item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Tigers’ Riley Greene Adds Another Prestigious Nomination to His Resume

item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Tigers made one of their best draft choices in the 2019 MLB Draft, taking outfielder Riley Greene with the fifth overall pick. Since Greene debuted for the Tigers, he's become known as the face of the offense, collecting multiple achievements along the way.
A three-time All-Star from 2024 to 2026, a Silver Slugger Award winner in 2025, and a reliable defender, Greene leads the Detroit offense into the future. It was proof enough when Greene went down with an injury in August that this offense needs him, but that's a good thing to have within the organization.
With the offseason in full swing for the Tigers, nominations for the prestigious Hank Aaron Award have been released as the playoffs continue.
The Hank Aaron Award is awarded annually to the best overall offensive performer in each league. The award was introduced in 1999 to mark the 25th anniversary of Hank Aaron breaking Babe Ruth's all-time home run record. A panel of Hall of Famers combines with a fan vote to determine the winners.
Of the 10 American League players representing 10 American League teams, Greene takes center stage for the Tigers organization.
How to Vote for Riley Greene
Greene finished his 2026 campaign with 21 home runs, 75 RBIs and an OPS of .844. While his home run and RBI totals were down from his 2025 campaign, the All-Star outfielder set a new career-high in OPS and doubles with 32.
Voting is open through Oct. 12, and Greene needs all the votes he can get from Tigers fans. Some of his biggest competitors for the award this season are Yordan Alvarez of the Houston Astros, Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays, and Ben Rice of the New York Yankees.
Of all the American League nominees, Greene ranked ninth in home runs, ninth in RBIs, and seventh in OPS. If Greene brings home the hardware, he will become the first Tigers player to do so since Miguel Cabrera won the award in back-to-back MVP seasons in 2012 and 2013.
If Greene doesn't win, it doesn't take away from how much improvement he had in 2026. A big flaw in Greene's game was strikeouts, punching out the most in Major League Baseball in 2025 with 201. He lowered that total to 157 in 2026 and improved his overall offense.
Greene is easily the top candidate to get a contract extension to ensure Detroit has a well-rounded athlete on their roster for years to come.
Dominic Minchella is a 2024 Eastern Michigan University graduate with a BA in Communications, Media, and Theatre Arts and a Journalism minor. He covers Major League Baseball for On SI and spends his free time watching games and sharing his insights.

item.content:encoded:
Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation
Pitching wins championships.
While that old adage still holds true, it has taken on a slightly different meaning in today's game, as teams need to successfully utilize their entire pitching staff to make a deep playoff run, rather than simply leaning on two or three starting pitchers to shoulder the load.
Still, a strong performance from the starting staff can give a team a major leg up. The Los Angeles Dodgers were the perfect example of that last October.
Ahead, we've ranked the playoff rotations of every postseason team. Which team's rotation is best positioned heading into the playoffs?
12. Houston Astros
1 of 12
RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.26 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 120 K, 102.0 IP)
RHP Hayden Wesneski (5-2, 3.50 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 41 K, 54.0 IP)
RHP Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.87 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 153 K, 153.2 IP)
RHP Ethan Pecko (1-0, 4.31 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 21 K, 31.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Ronel Blanco, RHP Cristian Javier (out for ALWC)
The Astros have used 19 different starting pitchers this year while navigating a long list of injuries. The fact that reliever AJ Blubaugh ranks third on the team with 95.1 innings pitched speaks volumes.
Ace Hunter Brown was slowed by a shoulder strain in the first half of the season, but he has returned to form with a 3.11 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 66.2 innings since the All-Star break.
With Cristian Javier making an early exit from his start on Wednesday, the rotation behind Brown is entirely up in the air. Hayden Wesneski and Peter Lambert are both capable of tossing a quality start, but they are short on big-game experience and could also be susceptible to a quick hook, shifting the focus to a Houston bullpen that ranks 17th in the majors with a 4.09 ERA.
11. Chicago White Sox
2 of 12
RHP Sean Burke (10-7, 3.40 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, 178 K, 167.0 IP)
RHP Davis Martin (9-7, 3.84 ERA, 1.29 WHIP, 121 K, 145.1 IP)
RHP Erick Fedde (8-9, 3.83 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 99 K, 141.0 IP)
LHP Anthony Kay (9-9, 4.53 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 125 K, 153.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Luis Castillo, RHP David Sandlin
The White Sox rank 26th in starters' ERA (4.62) and 28th in quality starts (34), so the starting rotation is something they will need to figure out how to navigate in the postseason rather than a strength.
Sean Burke and Davis Martin have accounted for 21 of those 33 quality starts. They will be asked to chew up innings at the top of the rotation, while games outside of their starts will likely be an all-hands-on-deck situation.
Sean Newcomb (58 G, 6 GS, 3.17 ERA, 88.0 IP) and Grant Taylor (59 G, 4 GS, 2.30 ERA, 82.0 IP) are both capable of providing length out of the bullpen, while deadline pickup Luis Castillo has also been shifted to a relief role.
10. Chicago Cubs
3 of 12
LHP Shota Imanaga (11-10, 3.74 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 173.1 IP)
RHP Kevin Gausman (4-2, 4.83 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 57 K, 50.1 IP)
LHP Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 96 K, 126.2 IP)
LHP David Peterson (6-2, 3.94 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, 68 K, 75.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Clay Holmes, RHP Javier Assad
The Cubs roll into October with arguably the best offense and best defense in baseball, but questions about their pitching staff hang over their postseason outlook.
Shota Imanaga has a 1.96 ERA and a 23-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 23 innings in September. That should put him in line to be the ace of the staff in October.
Veteran Kevin Gausman's significant playoff experience, including starting Game 2 and Game 6 of the World Series a year ago, should earn him a prominent role in the playoffs. At the back of the staff, Clay Holmes is the obvious candidate to shift to the bullpen given his past experience closing games.
9. San Diego Padres
4 of 12
RHP Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 159 K, 185.0 IP)
RHP Nick Pivetta (3-2, 2.86 ERA, 1.01 WHIP, 42 K, 34.2 IP)
RHP Walker Buehler (9-6, 4.56 ERA, 1.34 WHIP, 128 K, 150.0 IP)
LHP Robbie Ray (3-2, 5.02 ERA, 1.54 WHIP, 33 K, 43.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Casey Mize, RHP Randy Vásquez
The Padres rank fourth in the majors and top among projected playoff teams with 666.0 innings of work from their bullpen. That relief corps, anchored by Mason Miller and Adrian Morejón, will be a major factor in October.
Michael King is the clear ace of the staff. Nick Pivetta has pitched well since returning on Sept. 7, with 11 hits and three earned runs allowed in 14 innings over three starts.
Behind them, Walker Buehler is the logical Game 3 candidate, given his postseason resume and 3.15 ERA over 45.2 innings in his last nine starts. Deadline pickups Robbie Ray and Casey Mize have struggled since coming to San Diego and could be X-factors if they advance beyond the Wild Card Round.
8. Cleveland Guardians
5 of 12
RHP Gavin Williams (14-8, 3.63 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 244 K, 181.0 IP)
LHP Parker Messick (12-9, 2.55 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 191 K, 183.1 IP)
RHP Tanner Bibee (6-15, 4.35 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 142 K, 182.0 IP)
LHP Joey Cantillo (11-9, 3.62 ERA, 1.42 WHIP, 171 K, 159.0 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Foster Griffin
Gavin Williams leads the AL with 244 strikeouts and Parker Messick has a 2.27 ERA in 71.1 innings since the All-Star break, giving the Guardians a legitimate one-two punch to lead the way in the postseason.
Opening Day starter Tanner Bibee has struggled, posting an 8.24 ERA over 19.2 innings in September, but his track record still makes him the most likely candidate to start Game 3.
The question then becomes who gets the nod between Foster Griffin and Joey Cantillo. Griffin has a 5.19 ERA in nine starts since he was acquired at the trade deadline, while Cantillo has better surface-level results but has issued an AL-leading 81 walks in 159 innings.
7. Atlanta Braves
6 of 12
LHP Chris Sale (14-9, 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 200 K, 162.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Mahle (4-1, 1.99 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 48 K, 54.1 IP)
RHP Grant Holmes (10-5, 3.47 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, 114 K, 147.2 IP)
RHP JR Ritchie (1-4, 4.79 ERA, 1.46 WHIP, 66 K, 67.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Bryce Elder, RHP AJ Smith-Shawver, LHP Martín Pérez (out for NLWC)
Starting pitching was expected to be a glaring issue for the Braves when Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Hurston Waldrep and AJ Smith-Shawver all began the season on the injured list.
Instead, Chris Sale has put together a Cy Young-caliber season, while journeyman veterans Martín Pérez and Grant Holmes have combined for a 3.26 ERA in 289.2 innings spanning 55 starts. However, Pérez was just placed on the injured list with lower back inflammation, making a bullpen game the likely approach to fill the fourth starter role if they advance to the NLDS.
Deadline pickup Tyler Mahle has given them the No. 2 starter they still lacked, while a healthy Bryce Elder could be an X-factor if they advance deeper into October.
6. Milwaukee Brewers
7 of 12
RHP Jacob Misiorowski (15-5, 1.86 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 247 K, 169.1 IP)
RHP Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 110 K, 98.1 IP)
LHP Robert Gasser (5-5, 4.01 ERA, 1.24 WHIP, 94 K, 103.1 IP)
RHP Dustin May (2-2, 5.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 33 K, 33.2 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Kyle Harrison, LHP Shane Drohan
Jacob Misiorowski pitched out of the bullpen for the Brewers last October, posting a 1.50 ERA, 0.83 WHIP and 16 strikeouts in 12 innings across three appearances. He is now poised to lead their staff this postseason.
Rookie Logan Henderson has not allowed more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts this season. He is 8-2 with a 2.19 ERA and 0.79 WHIP in 70 innings since the All-Star break.
Left-hander Robert Gasser has a 1.71 ERA in 26.1 innings over his last five appearances. He will be a significant part of manager Pat Murphy's plan of mixing and matching innings behind Misiorowski and Henderson.
5. Boston Red Sox
8 of 12
RHP Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 149 K, 169.0 IP)
LHP Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 140 K, 148.1 IP)
LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP)
RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.49 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 90 K, 112.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Jake Bennett, LHP Patrick Sandoval
Few offseason additions have made a bigger impact than Sonny Gray, who has 20 quality starts in 29 games this year and is on track for his fourth career top-10 finish in Cy Young voting for four different teams.
Rookie Payton Tolle has been the team's most consistent starter behind Gray this year and will factor into the playoff rotation, while high-priced offseason signing Ranger Suarez has a 1.09 ERA over 24.2 innings in September.
The X-factor could be Brayan Bello after he threw a gem (8.0 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 11 K) on the road against the Rays on Sept. 19. He has a 2.28 ERA over 51.1 innings while working mostly out of the bullpen since returning from a minor league demotion before the All-Star break, but he is stretched back out to start.
4. Tampa Bay Rays
9 of 12
RHP Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 174 K, 172.0 IP)
RHP Nick Martinez (15-5, 2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 108 K, 177.1 IP)
RHP Freddy Peralta (4-2, 3.60 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 39 K, 50.0 IP)
RHP Griffin Jax (8-10, 3.62 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 115 K, 109.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Ian Seymour, LHP Shane McClanahan (out for ALDS)
Few organizations do a better job fully utilizing the entire pitching staff than the Rays, but this October they have three legitimate rotation anchors who can get them deep into games in Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and deadline pickup Freddy Peralta.
That group gets even deeper if Shane McClanahan returns to action, though he has already been ruled out for the ALDS. Even if he's not able to return, reliever-turned-starter Griffin Jax has also been quietly excellent this season with a 3.23 ERA and 105 strikeouts in 100.1 innings over his 22 starts.
They could still opt to utilize an opener when it makes sense, or piggyback one of their starters with left-hander Ian Seymour if the situation arises. This isn't a staff that needs to lean on multiple bullpen games to get through a series.
3. Philadelphia Phillies
10 of 12
LHP Cristopher Sánchez (18-6, 2.93 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 221 K, 200.0 IP)
RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 3.06 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 188 K, 156.0 IP)
RHP Aaron Nola (7-11, 4.54 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 177 K, 174.1 IP)
LHP Jesús Luzardo (14-5, 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 221 K, 178.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Andrew Painter
Jesús Luzardo played catch earlier this week as he works his way back from shoulder inflammation, though his postseason status remains up in the air. There's a chance he will be limited to bullpen work early in the playoffs.
Veteran Aaron Nola has hit his stride of late, posting a 2.45 ERA in 66 innings over his last 11 starts, so he can fill the void behind the dynamic one-two punch of Cristopher Sánchez (7.7 WAR, 1st among all SP) and Zack Wheeler (5.6 WAR, 8th among all SP).
The Phillies rank second in the majors with 73 quality starts and 869.1 innings from their starting staff, so they are poised to lean on their starters as hard as anyone in October.
2. New York Yankees
11 of 12
RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP, 239 K, 193.2 IP)
LHP Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA, 0.99 WHIP, 104 K, 112.2 IP)
RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 131 K, 127.0 IP)
LHP Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 91 K, 84.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Will Warren
With AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and three established veteran starters capable of frontline production in Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón, the Yankees rotation is capable of making a major impact in October.
Schlittler logged a 1.26 ERA over 14.1 innings last October, including eight scoreless frames against the rival Red Sox in the Wild Card Round. He will now be asked to shoulder a heavier load.
It remains to be seen who the odd-man out would be in a series that calls for a three-man staff, though Rodón has made his case with a 1.42 ERA, 0.75 WHIP and 28 strikeouts in 25.1 innings in September.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
12 of 12
RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-9, 2.53 ERA, 0.87 WHIP, 182 K, 185.0 IP)
LHP Tarik Skubal (4-2, 2.95 ERA, 1.13 WHIP, 60 K, 55.0 IP)
LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.86 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, 52 K, 38.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Glasnow (5-2, 3.53 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 98 K, 74.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Emmet Sheehan, LHP Justin Wrobleski
The Dodgers have once again navigated much of the regular season without Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, but they are healthy rolling into October and poised to round out the playoff rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto and deadline pickup Tarik Skubal.
The starting rotation logged a 2.68 ERA over 104 innings last postseason, with Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow starting 13 of 17 games and the rest going to Shohei Ohtani, who will be limited to DH duties but has been sufficiently replaced by a two-time Cy Young winner in Skubal.
Right-hander Emmet Sheehan has a 0.53 ERA and 24 strikeouts over 17 innings in three September starts. He will serve as a multi-inning weapon out of the bullpen.

item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] Boston Red Sox Have Clear Offseason Need
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe
item.description: The Boston Red Sox offense delivered a disastrous performance in the Wild Card round of the playoffs, getting outscored 18-2 en route to a two-game sweep by the New York Yankees. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox offense delivered a disastrous performance in the Wild Card round of the playoffs, getting outscored 18-2 en route to a two-game sweep by the New York Yankees. After an anemic final month of the regular season, one thing is clear: the Red Sox must replace the power they traded away with Rafael Devers in 2025.
In the Red Sox's four World Series wins since 2000, they have consistently been among baseball's best offenses. In 2004, they ranked first in runs (949), fifth in home runs (222), first in OPS (.832), and first in WRC+ plus (114). In 2007, they were fourth in runs (867), 18th in home runs (166), third in OPS (.806), and second in wRC+ (109). The theme continues in 2013, when they led the league in runs (853), were sixth in home runs (178), first in OPS (.795), and first in wRC+ (114). Finally, the 2018 Red Sox were first in runs (876), ninth in home runs (208), first in OPS (.792), and fourth in wRC+ (111).
Of course, for the first three World Series titles, Boston had Hall of Fame designated hitter David Ortiz in the lineup, and the 2018 team posted the best record in franchise history en route to a title. However, this trend isn't isolated to the Red Sox; over the last five years, each World Series-winning team (Dodgers, Rangers, Astros, Braves) ranked top 10 in those four categories.
The idea that power wins you games in the playoffs isn't new, and Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow isn't unaware of it; it was among the first things he said at the 2025 GM Meetings. "I don't want to get so anchored to this idea that the only way to score runs is home runs. We showed that isn't the case. That said, a disproportionate number of runs in the postseason are scored via the home run, and that's not something that we can ignore," said Breslow.
The theory that runs are scored disproportionately via home runs played out in the Wild Card round against the Yankees, who scored nine of their 18 runs on home runs. The Red Sox themselves scored their only two runs of the series via a pair of solo home runs.
Yet, heading into 2026, the Red Sox offense clearly was a bat short, and that proved to be the case throughout the regular season as they finished the year 23rd in runs (689), 26th in home runs (163), 19th in OPS (717), and 17th in wRC+ (99).
A Rafael Devers-sized hole in the lineup
Unfortunately for Breslow and the Red Sox, a massive hole remains in the heart of the lineup where Devers once stood. In his first full season in San Francisco, the former Red Sox slugger hit .258/.340/.525/.865 with a career-high 37 home runs and 98 RBI on one of the worst teams in baseball. Adding Devers' home run total to Boston's would have vaulted them into the top 10 in baseball. Beyond providing a massive power boost to the Boston offense, Devers would also have stabilized the designated hitter spot, where the Red Sox got some of the worst production in baseball.
Devers also has a strong track record of success in the postseason, where he's hit .303/.382/.573/.955 with eight home runs in 26 games, and against the Yankees, against whom he posted .269/.346/.527/.873 in 122 games.
Regardless, Devers was traded, and he is not coming back. However, the team had to replace Devers' impact in the lineup, and ultimately they failed to do that. Willson Contreras had a career year in 2026, but he still profiles much more as a complementary piece to the guy in the lineup rather than being the guy himself.
Plenty of power options were available in free agency ahead of the 2026 season, including Pete Alonso, Kyle Schwarber, and even Alex Bregman. However, ultimately Breslow showed little interest in Schwarber, lost a bidding war to the Baltimore Orioles for Alonso, and was unwilling to include a no-trade clause in contract negotiations to retain Bregman. Instead, pivoting to building the team around strong pitching and defense.
Now that both pitching and defense are in place, Breslow needs to focus on adding power to the lineup because the overwhelming sample size shows that slugging leads to postseason success.

item.description: With the Wild Card round of the 2026 MLB Playoffs behind us, it's time for the Division Series to get underway. It all starts on Saturday with all four Division Series matchups. With that in mind, we polled the Rotoworld Baseball staff for their thoughts on how the rest of the postseason will play out. item.content:encoded:
With the Wild Card round of the 2026 MLB Playoffs behind us, it's time for the Division Series to get underway. It all starts on Saturday with all four Division Series matchups.
With that in mind, we polled the Rotoworld Baseball staff for their thoughts on how the rest of the postseason will play out. Check out our picks and analysis for the Division Series, Championship Series, and World Series.
The 2026 MLB postseason has arrived. Stay up to date with the latest results and more.
2026 ALDS, NLDS Predictions
| Writer | White Sox vs. Guardians | Yankees vs. Rays | Braves vs. Dodgers | Padres vs. Brewers |
| Eric Samulski | Guardians | Yankees | Dodgers | Brewers |
| Matthew Pouliot | Guardians | Yankees | Dodgers | Brewers |
| David Shovein | Guardians | Rays | Dodgers | Brewers |
| Christopher Crawford | White Sox | Yankees | Dodgers | Padres |
| D.J. Short | Guardians | Yankees | Dodgers | Padres |
White Sox vs. Guardians
Crawford: I don't think there's much of a difference between the White Sox and the Guardians. I think the fact that the White Sox already won a pair of postseason games on the road, both relatively convincingly, is something working in their favor. I can't quite go team of destiny or any of that stuff, but there does seem to be something about this White Sox team. I realize that's not exactly the most scientific answer, but my heart believes in the Chicago Popes.
Yankees vs. Rays
Short: The Rays and Yankees are set to meet in the postseason for the second time ever, and the first with actual fans in the building. While the Rays were the better regular season team this year, I think the Yankees are better built for the postseason. It starts with the rotation, which was the best in the majors with a 3.30 ERA, but their bullpen was even better with a 3.15 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has dominated the Yankees in his career, but New York has a level of rotation depth the Rays simply can't match.
Aaron Judge's status for the ALDS remains uncertain because of his calf injury, but even without him, one could argue that the Yankees have the more dangerous lineup. Their ability to change the game with one swing is something I think will win out over Tampa Bay's small-ball style in a short series.
Braves vs. Dodgers
Pouliot: Atlanta's pitching staff received 7 2/3 innings from Chris Sale and seven from Tyler Mahle and still seemed hard-pressed to get through the three-game Wild Card series against the Phillies. How are they going to hold up without those two to start the series against the Dodgers? Even without the relief appearance Thursday, starting Sale in Game 2 would have required pitching him on four days' rest, which he hasn't done since early April. As is, it looks like Sale in Game 3 and Mahle in Game 4. Maybe the Dodgers' bats start off cold and the Braves can steal a game in Los Angeles, but as shorthanded as they are in terms of pitching depth, not having their rotation lined puts them at a major disadvantage.
Padres vs. Brewers
Samulski: The Padres have been red hot and dominated the Cubs, but I published an article before the postseason with research from the last 10 years that showed teams coming into the playoffs with tons of momentum don't meaningfully perform better than teams who struggle coming into the postseason. I might as well trust my own research. The Brewers have been arguably the best team in baseball all season. Their lineup is incredibly tough to get out, and they have possibly the deepest overall pitching staff in the postseason.
Full MLB Postseason Predictions
| Writer | ALCS Winner | NLCS Winner | World Series Champion |
| Eric Samulski | New York Yankees | Milwaukee Brewers | Milwaukee Brewers |
| Matthew Pouliot | New York Yankees | Los Angeles Dodgers | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| David Shovein | Tampa Bay Rays | Milwaukee Brewers | Tampa Bay Rays |
| Christopher Crawford | New York Yankees | San Diego Padres | San Diego Padres |
| D.J. Short | New York Yankees | San Diego Padres | New York Yankees |
Samulski: I will admit my bias again when talking about why I picked against the Yankees. I just think this Brewers team is finally going to break through. The Yankees were lights out against the Red Sox, but they have been prone to strikeouts throughout the season. That can make them a volatile offense, and I think the consistency of the Brewers will win the day here.
Pouliot: A few weeks ago, I might have picked another champ, but with the Dodgers' bullpen rounding into form, their biggest potential weakness seems gone. Edwin Díaz still isn't a sure thing, but he was much improved after coming off the IL, allowing just one hit and one walk while striking out nine in his final five innings. Roki Sasaki and Evan Phillips both hit 100 mph last week, and Kris Bubic, if he's even needed, could prove to be a secret weapon. Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman might not be able to carry the offense at this point, but even if the Dodgers are lacking their usual firepower, they should be able to win some low-scoring games.
Crawford: I don't think the Padres are the best team in baseball. I don't think they're even the best team in their division. But I love the way they're playing now, and that bullpen, quality starters at the top of the rotation and just enough star power makes me believe they're built for the postseason, and their first-ever World Series championship.
Short: I love the Yankees' pitching and Aaron Judge should be back eventually in some capacity, which only improves the team's outlook for a potential World Series matchup. As opposed to their meeting in 1998, I would expect the Padres to make this one much more competitive. San Diego's offense has been great in the second half and their bullpen is positively scary. Still, the Yankees would hold the major edge in starting pitching, and that would ultimately make the difference in my hypothetical World Series matchup.

item.title: [Chicago Tribune] Column: Can the Chicago White Sox keep succeeding in the postseason without a conventional rotation?

item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND — If you’re a baseball fan of a certain age, you’ve probably spent most of your life knowing some certainties about a pitching staff.
The five best guys (or four if you’re really old) are the starters who will try to get you through the bulk of the game. The best reliever is the closer, who pitches the last inning or possibly part of the eighth if he’s dominant enough. The next-best relievers — preferably one left-hander and one right-hander — are the setup men, the potential bridges from starter to closer.
And the pitcher who is least effective on the staff is the mop-up man, whose main function is keeping the better relievers from being overused.
For years managers used that basic blueprint, or something close to it, to get through the regular season. Then when the playoffs arrived, the best three or four starters went longer because the season was almost over and they could empty their bullets in the biggest games.
But baseball has changed, for better or worse, and now anything goes. Boston Red Sox ace Sonny Gray was removed in the fifth inning of a do-or-die wild-card game Wednesday, and Gray and his teammates grumbled about how the game got to this point.
Which brings us to the 2026 Chicago White Sox, who are trying to win with a “no-rotation” rotation.
Will Venable, the second-year White Sox manager, announced Friday that left-handed reliever Hagen Smith would start Game 1 of the American League Division Series against the Cleveland Guardians, serving as the opener Saturday, as he did in pitching three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the wild-card win in Houston.
It’s no surprise. The Sox have used openers a league-leading 32 times this season, including Smith’s outing Tuesday. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.
But does the no-rotation rotation have its limits, or can Venable’s Sox keep succeeding in the postseason with a bullpen-first strategy?
Venable acknowledged Sean Burke could start Game 2 on Monday, as he did in a four-inning start in Game 2 against the Astros, in which starters Anthony Kay and Erick Fedde both pitched in relief. But other than Burke, it might be a guessing game from here on out.
Can Smith come back to start Game 3 at home Wednesday, giving him three starts in their first five playoff games? Who knows what’s up Venable’s sleeve?
“I think the way it’s set up with these off days, we’re going to leverage the arms that we want to leverage when we want to use them throughout these first couple,” Venable said. “And if that means that one of the guys who we’ve been giving starts to throughout the season takes a bulk role in that, there’s certainly potential for that. But I think you can expect us to mix and match and use our best arms in the most optimal way.”
That suggests Smith and Grant Taylor can be the designated bookends of multiple games, with Jordan Hicks, David Sandlin and Sean Newcomb in the middle and Kay, Fedde and Davis Martin as the wild cards.
It’s almost the polar-opposite approach that then-manager Ozzie Guillén employed in the 2005 postseason, when José Contreras, Mark Buehrle, Freddy Garcia and Jon Garland combined for a 2.84 ERA in 12 starts, leading the Sox on an 11-1 run to their World Series title.
In the five-game win over the Anaheim Angels in the AL Championship Series, the four starters had four straight complete games and combined for 44 1/3 of the 45 total innings, with Neal Cotts contributing the other two outs in the ninth inning of the Game 1 loss. The rest of the bullpen had a nice seat to watch the starters dealing.
“I don’t know if you’ll ever see that again,” Sox catcher A.J. Pierzynski said afterward. “Managers just don’t do that anymore. They don’t have confidence to let guys go 120 pitches and throw nine innings.”
In the World Series, advance scout Bryan Little and his crew gave Guillén and pitching coach Don Cooper a near-perfect report on strengths and weaknesses of the Astros hitters. Contreras and Buerhle both went seven innings in the first two wins at Sox Park, and Garland went seven in Game 3 in Houston before the Astros tied it off Dustin Hermanson in the eighth.
Guillén was forced to use his well-rested bullpen when the game went 14 innings but also used Orlando “El Duque” Hernández and Buehrle. After Geoff Blum’s go-ahead home run in the 14th, Buehrle notched the infamous “buzzed save” by getting the final out after having a few beers in the clubhouse. “No more than three … I swear,” he later said.
Buehrle wound up on a Wheaties box, but he didn’t become a legend for his cereal-eating habits.
Game 4 was as old-school as it gets, with Garcia going seven shutout innings, Cliff Politte and Cotts getting the Sox through the eighth and Bobby Jenks closing out a 1-0 win to start the parade plans.
“That type of game is like the ones I watched for 162 games during the regular season,” Guillén said in the celebratory clubhouse.
Venable’s approach in the postseason also mirrors what he has done for much of the season.
General manager Chris Getz knew he didn’t have a dominant rotation in spring training, and opening-day starter Shane Smith was quickly dispatched to Triple-A Charlotte after three starts. Martin, Burke, Kay and Fedde have been the mainstays, though Fedde, who signed at the start of spring training, had only 15 starts in his 33 games.
Taylor has evolved into the de facto closer but can go three innings if needed. He also was used as an opener in April. Seranthony Domínguez led the team 12 saves, even after being dispatched at the trade deadline.
Openers aren’t a new concept. “Bullpenning” has been around for the last decade. Cubs manager Craig Counsell also used openers in last year’s postseason.
But is it possible no team has been as unconventional as the ’26 Sox in this particular run?
“It’s possible,” Getz said during the wild-card celebration. “We weren’t trying to re-create the wheel. We were trying to optimize the group that we had. So much of (baseball) has relied on starting pitching. We would’ve liked to do that. But if we were trying to win games, we had to lean on the strength of the club, and we’ve done that.”
The Sox’s strategy has been criticized, especially when an opener puts the bulk pitcher in a hole. Guillén himself has said on the Chicago Sports Network he’s not a fan of openers.
But if the Sox go all the way without a true rotation, the players may never have to buy a meal or drink in Chicago again. Or at least that’s the adage.
“More often than not I’ll just roll in and buy a drink or buy my dinner,” Blum told me last week in Houston. “But every so often, if there is a hard-core Sox fan in the bar or in the restaurant, there will be a free drink that will show up once in a while.”
So it’s kind of true?
“It still carries a little bit of weight,” Blum said. “We’re not quite the ’85 Bears, but the ’05 Sox do OK.”

item.content:encoded:
Philadelphia Phillies second baseman Luis Arraez issued a statement to the team’s fans following the end of his first season with the team.
Arraez, who began the season with the San Francisco Giants, was traded to the Phillies at the MLB trade deadline as the team tried to make a deep postseason run with his bat in their lineup.
While Arraez was excellent for the Giants, he struggled a bit with the Phillies after the trade, and to make matters worse, he got injured in late September and was forced to miss the Phillies’ National League Wild Card series against the Atlanta Braves, which they lost 2-1 in a three-game set.
Still, he loved his time in Philadelphia.
Luis Arraez Issues Statement After Phillies’ Season Ends
Taking to his social media, Arraez issued a lengthy statement where he thanked the Phillies’ fans for making him feel at home for the past two months.
“Philadelphia. When I was traded to the Phillies in the middle of the season, I didn’t know what to expect. But from day one, you welcomed me with open arms and made me feel at home.Playing at Citizens Bank Park in front of a sea of red and feeling your energy is something I’ll never forget. I wanted nothing more than to finish the season on the field with my teammates. Watching the playoffs from the bench because of an injury was incredibly difficult, because all I wanted was to be out there fighting alongside them. Thank you, Phillies fans, for all your support and for making my time in Philadelphia so special. — Luis. Philadelphia,” Arraez wrote in an Instagram post.
Luis Arraez Is an Impending Free Agent
A free agent once again this winter, Arraez will be highly coveted after having an overall terrific season, one where he finished second in the NL batting title race with a .310 batting average, just one point behind the winner, Arizona Diamondbacks catcher Gabriel Moreno.
Overall, Arraez batted .310 with a .765 OPS and a 127 OPS+ on the season, though his numbers after being traded to the Phillies declined as he struggled with his new team. Even still, his final numbers for the season saw him tally a solid 2.9 bWAR.
Not only did Arraez have good overall numbers at the plate this year, but his glovework at second base also improved greatly after he was routinely criticized for his defense during the last several seasons, which included being moved to first base when he played for the San Diego Padres last year.
The Phillies will likely attempt to keep Arraez for next season and beyond, but he will likely get some very lucrative contract offers during free agency, so it’s no guarantee that he returns to the Phillies.
That being said, he obviously had a great experience playing in Philadelphia based on what he wrote in this statement, so if the team and the player’s agent can come to terms on a fair contract for both sides, then perhaps he will return to “The City of Brotherly Love” next season.

item.dc:creator: Chris Spiering; ClutchPoints

item.content:encoded:
Why Royals' Vinnie Pasquantino believes White Sox are 'built' for playoffs appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Vinnie Pasquantino has spent enough time facing the Chicago White Sox to know their bullpen presents a tougher task than the name recognition might suggest. That experience has the Kansas City Royals first baseman believing Chicago can push the Cleveland Guardians to the limit in the ALDS.
The White Sox head into Saturday afternoon's opener after sweeping the Houston Astros in the Wild Card round. Pasquantino sees a pitching staff capable of helping them extend that postseason run.
"In my opinion, the White Sox are built for these series because they can just go to the bullpen," Pasquantino said on The Rich Eisen Show. "If you look at some of the names in the bullpen, as a casual fan or if you don't know the White Sox, you don't think much of it. But having faced these guys, it is uncomfortable at-bats; their pitching coach does a great job…"
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"I do think the White Sox are alive in this series for sure."
—@VPasquantino on the White Sox ahead of their series against the Guardians ⚾️
(via @RichEisenShow) pic.twitter.com/RMXt0MCWmC
— SportsCenter (@SportsCenter) October 2, 2026
That assessment carries weight coming from a division opponent. Pasquantino's confidence comes from standing in the batter's box against those pitchers, where unfamiliar names can quickly become difficult matchups.
A reliable bullpen also gives Chicago flexibility in a short series. The White Sox can turn to relief options when a starter struggles or a matchup calls for a change, rather than waiting for an inning to get away from them.
But Pasquantino identified a complication: Cleveland knows those arms, too.
"The disadvantage is that they are playing a team they have played all year. If anyone is going to know the White Sox, it's the Guardians," he said. "I think this series will go five. Whoever plays the little things better will win that series. I do think the White Sox are alive in this series for sure."
The regular-season results support his expectation of a close matchup. Chicago edged Cleveland 7-6, with only a one-run differential between the teams.
Related: White Sox reveal who will pitch against Guardians' Parker Messick in ALDS Game 1
Related: 3 bold predictions for White Sox-Guardians ALDS clash

item.content:encoded:
For the Sixth Consecutive Year, TelevisaUnivision’s Sports Audio Network Will Deliver Live, Play-by-Play Coverage of the MLB Playoffs Through the 122nd World Series Across All Platforms.
Courtesy: TelevisaUnivision
MIAMI, FL. – October 2, 2026 – TUDN Radio, the premier Hispanic sports audio network of TelevisaUnivision, will once again serve as the exclusive U.S. Spanish-language radio home for the 2026 Major League Baseball Postseason. Marking the network’s sixth consecutive edition delivering October baseball to Hispanic audiences across the nation, fans can experience the entire postseason journey entirely in Spanish—from the opening pitch of the Wild Card Series through the final out of the historic 122nd World Series.
Continuing its long-standing collaboration with Major League Baseball, TUDN Radio will bring every moment of the postseason to life, led by the voices of acclaimed announcers Luis Quiñones, Alberto “El Beto” Ferreiro, Daniel Alvarez, and Jesus Acosta. This elite broadcast team will provide unparalleled coverage across the network’s nationwide terrestrial radio footprint, as well as digitally via the Uforia app and TUDN’s digital platforms.
“Baseball holds a deep, passionate connection with our Hispanic audience, and we are incredibly proud to return for our sixth postseason as the exclusive Spanish-language audio voice of MLB,” said Carlos F. Azcarate, VP of Sports Radio Network. “We are thrilled to continue bringing fans closer to the diamond, delivering every pivotal moment, dramatic home run, and championship celebration directly to them, wherever they choose to listen.”
Unprecedented Coverage Across All Platforms
TUDN Radio will broadcast key matchups throughout each round of the postseason, culminating in comprehensive Spanish-language audio coverage of the entire Fall Classic. Listeners can tune in across multiple touchpoints:
- TUDN Radio Network: Broadcast across affiliate radio stations in primary Hispanic markets nationwide.
- The Uforia App: TelevisaUnivision’s audio platform, offering live streaming on mobile devices across the United States.
- TUDN.com and TUDN App: Live digital audio integration for fans following games online.
- Smart Speakers & Connected Devices: Voice-activated live streaming through supported home integrations.
The 2026 Postseason Schedule on TUDN Radio
TUDN Radio’s coverage will feature full pre-game, play-by-play, and post-game analysis across every round:
- MLB Wild Card Series: Complete coverage of the best-of-three opening rounds.
- American League and National League Division Series (ALDS & NLDS): In-depth coverage as teams battle for the pennant.
- American League and National League Championship Series (ALCS & NLCS): Live calls deciding the champions of each league.
- The 122nd World Series: Uninterrupted, full-series coverage of baseball’s championship showdown.
Adding to the comprehensive live game broadcasts, fans can catch all the surrounding excitement, expert breakdowns, and exclusive player interviews on TUDN Radio’s premier baseball show, Desde El Diamante.
Complete broadcast schedules, station directories, and talent assignments will be updated throughout the month as matchups advance. Fans can follow along with live game updates, highlights, and behind-the-scenes content on X, Instagram, and Facebook via @TUDNRadio and by visiting TUDN.com.
CONTACT:
Melissa Agudelo – Director of Communications, News & Sports
###
TUDN Radio Regresa como la Casa Radial Exclusiva en Español en EE. UU. para la Postemporada de la MLB 2026
Por sexto año consecutivo, la cadena de audio deportivo de TelevisaUnivision ofrecerá cobertura en vivo, narración jugada a jugada y análisis de los Playoffs de la MLB hasta la 122.ª Serie Mundial en todas sus plataformas
Cortesía: TelevisaUnivision
MIAMI, Florida – 2 de octubre de 2026 – TUDN Radio, la principal cadena de audio deportivo para la audiencia hispana de TelevisaUnivision, volverá a ser la casa exclusiva de radio en español en EE. UU. de la Postemporada de las Grandes Ligas 2026. Por sexto año consecutivo, la cadena llevará el beisbol de octubre a las audiencias hispanas de todo el país, permitiéndoles vivir de principio a fin la emoción de la postemporada en español, desde el primer lanzamiento de la Serie de Comodines hasta el último out de la histórica 122.ª Serie Mundial.
Como parte de su colaboración de larga trayectoria con Major League Baseball, TUDN Radio llevará a los aficionados cada instante de la postemporada de la mano de los reconocidos narradores Luis Quiñones, Alberto “El Beto” Ferreiro, Daniel Alvarez y Jesús Acosta. Este destacado equipo de transmisión ofrecerá una cobertura de primer nivel a través de la red de estaciones de radio terrestre de la cadena en todo el país, así como en formato digital mediante la app de Uforia y las plataformas digitales de TUDN.
“El beisbol mantiene un vínculo profundo y apasionado con nuestra audiencia hispana, y nos llena de orgullo regresar por sexto año consecutivo como la voz exclusiva en español de la postemporada de la MLB”, afirmó Carlos F. Azcarate, VP de Sports Radio Network. “Nos entusiasma seguir acercando a los aficionados al diamante y llevarles cada momento decisivo, cada cuadrangular dramático y cada celebración del campeonato, sin importar dónde elijan escucharnos”.
Cobertura sin precedentes en todas las plataformas
TUDN Radio transmitirá los enfrentamientos más destacados de cada ronda de la postemporada, hasta llegar a una cobertura integral en audio en español de toda la Serie Mundial. Los aficionados podrán seguir la acción a través de múltiples plataformas:
- TUDN Radio Network: Transmisiones a través de estaciones afiliadas en los principales mercados hispanos de todo el país.
- La app de Uforia: La plataforma de audio de TelevisaUnivision ofrecerá streaming en vivo para dispositivos móviles en todo Estados Unidos.
- TUDN.com y la app de TUDN: Integración de audio digital en vivo para los aficionados que sigan los partidos por internet.
- Altavoces inteligentes y dispositivos conectados: Streaming en vivo mediante comandos de voz a través de las integraciones domésticas compatibles.
Calendario de la Postemporada 2026 en TUDN Radio
La cobertura de TUDN Radio incluirá previa, narración jugada a jugada y análisis posterior a cada encuentro durante todas las rondas de la postemporada:
- Serie de Comodines de la MLB: Cobertura completa de la ronda inaugural al mejor de tres juegos.
- Series Divisionales de la Liga Americana y la Liga Nacional (ALDS y NLDS): Análisis en profundidad mientras los equipos compiten por el campeonato de cada liga.
- Series de Campeonato de la Liga Americana y la Liga Nacional (ALCS y NLCS): Narración en vivo de los encuentros que definirán a los campeones de cada liga.
- 122.ª Serie Mundial: Cobertura ininterrumpida y de principio a fin de la gran batalla por el campeonato de las Grandes Ligas.
Además de las transmisiones en vivo de los partidos, los aficionados podrán disfrutar de toda la emoción alrededor de la postemporada, análisis especializados y entrevistas exclusivas con jugadores en Desde El Diamante, el programa insignia de beisbol de TUDN Radio.
Los calendarios completos de transmisiones, directorios de estaciones y asignaciones del talento se actualizarán durante el mes a medida que avancen los enfrentamientos. Los aficionados podrán seguir las novedades de los partidos en vivo, los mejores momentos y contenido exclusivo detrás de cámaras en X, Instagram y Facebook a través de @TUDNRadio, así como en TUDN.com.

item.dc:creator: Dallin Ballard
item.description: Alex Bregman has officially won the 2026 Rizzo Award, but the victory was far from a blowout. item.content:encoded:
Alex Bregman has officially won the 2026 Rizzo Award, but the victory was far from a blowout. According to Bleed Cubbie Blue, the new third baseman finished with a score of +26, just a half point ahead of Pete Crow-Armstrong. This marks the closest finish in the entire 13-year history of the award. The race was so tight that fans could only guess the winner until the very end of the season.
The Numbers That Tell the Story
The final standings show a massive gap between the top performers and the rest of the roster. Bregman led all free agent signings with his +26 mark, proving he was the most impactful new addition. Per Bleed Cubbie Blue, Crow-Armstrong followed closely with +25.5 as the top returning player. Ben Brown sat at +13.5, while the legendary Ian Happ and Aaron Civale both finished with +10. The top ten list is packed with talent, but the battle for first place was a genuine nail-biter.
At the other end of the spectrum, the bottom of the list tells a different story about the team's struggles. Nico Hoerner finished with -18, while Dansby Swanson landed at -17. Seiya Suzuki also ended up at -17, joining the group of players who had a rough season. The data shows a clear divide between the heroes who carried the team and the goats who dragged it down. Even the best teams have players who simply cannot find their footing when it matters most.
Why the Playoffs Changed Everything
The regular season heroics did not translate into a deep playoff run for the Cubs. The team was swept by the Padres in the Wild Card series, ending the season with barely a whimper. Bleed Cubbie Blue noted that the Cubs looked completely overmatched over those two days.
Despite the loss, the regular season data suggests the team was built to hit home runs. For almost the whole year, the roster stayed close to the top of the home run leaders. However, the playoffs exposed a lack of pitching depth that the regular season stats could not hide. The Padres had a clear plan and executed it perfectly against Cubs starter Matthew Boyd. They swung early and often, recognizing strikes and punishing mistakes. The Cubs needed a pitcher who could go seven innings against a good offense, and they simply did not have one.
Bregman's regular season success stands as a bright spot in an otherwise painful year. His +26 score proves he was the right choice for the club, even if the playoffs did not go as planned. The question now is whether the team can build on this individual success or if the roster needs a complete overhaul. The numbers do not lie about who helped the most, but the final score of the season remains the same. The Cubs are back to square one.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Braves’ Walt Weiss provides update on Chris Sale NLDS plan
item.dc:creator: Alex House; ClutchPoints

The Atlanta Braves have been meticulous in how they handle Chris Sale for the last three years, making sure to give him enough rest so that he can maintain his excellent form for an entire campaign. The 2024 National League Cy Young Award winner has still spent time on the injured list, but their plan has helped him become a top-tier starting pitcher
item.content:encoded:
Braves' Walt Weiss provides update on Chris Sale NLDS plan appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Atlanta Braves have been meticulous in how they handle Chris Sale for the last three years, making sure to give him enough rest so that he can maintain his excellent form for an entire campaign. The 2024 National League Cy Young Award winner has still spent time on the injured list, but their plan has helped him become a top-tier starting pitcher once again. All bets are off in the playoffs, though. Right?
Two days after starting Game 1 of the NL Wild Card Series versus the Philadelphia Phillies, Sale made it clear he wanted to take the mound in a do-or-die Game 3. Despite holding a 6-2 lead in the eighth inning, manager Walt Weiss brought in the veteran left-hander to finish off Atlanta's longtime rival. Sale indicated that he still plans to pitch against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday night, but nothing is official yet.
In fact, it sounds like there is serious doubt surrounding the 10-time All-Star's status for Game 2 of the NL Division Series. Although Weiss said a Sale start in LA is "still on the table," the Braves want their ace to be fresh enough for postseason battle.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"We're gonna err on the side of giving him (time to rest) if it's even close," the NL Manager of the Year candidate revealed, per ESPN's Alden Gonzalez. That statement is a far cry from Sale's confident remarks following Atlanta's series-clinching win over Philly. Weiss has been in baseball a long time, however.
It is possible the skipper is just engaging in some good old-fashioned gamesmanship before his squad faces the two-time reigning World Series champions. The Braves are a title contender in their own right, but they will want to gain a mental edge on the Dodgers if one is attainable. Disarming the home team with a surprise pitching move seems like the perfect gambit to try in October. Dave Roberts is a veteran of this game as well, though, so he may not be caught off guard.
Of course, there is a possibility that Walt Weiss is merely telling the truth. Perhaps Atlanta will wait until it returns to Truist Park to start Chris Sale. If so, then the team's bullpen move in Game 3 of the Wild Card round will seem even more puzzling.
One thing is for certain. Sale is a warrior who has openly expressed his desire to carry a big workload in the playoffs. We shall see if the Braves trust him to run wild in Chavez Ravine. The time for speculation will soon end. Game 1 of the NLDS begins on Saturday at 4 p.m. ET.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers postseason primer: Where do Shohei Ohtani and everyone else stand as they go for a three-peat?

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers' quest for a three-peat begins in earnest on Saturday with Game 1 of the NLDS, as they seek to become the first time since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees to complete a trilogy of titles.
Up to this point, the path for L.A. hasn't been entirely straightforward. There have been times when the Dodgers have looked a bit rickety, and that's to say nothing about everything happening off the field. They are also arguably the most talented team in the playoffs and are coming off another 100-win season.
No matter how you slice it, this is a club with more than its fair share of questions. Let's get into them, starting with the easier ones.
Who are the Dodgers playing in the NLDS?
The Dodgers will face the NL East champion Atlanta Braves, who defeated the Philadelphia Phillies in a three-game wild-card series. The Dodgers went 1-5 against Atlanta in the regular season, getting outscored 26-15.
The winner of the best-of-five series gets the victor of the other NLDS between the Milwaukee Brewers and San Diego Padres.
When do the Dodgers play?
Here's the full NLDS schedule:
| Game | Date | Time (ET) | Channel | Location |
| 1 | Oct. 3 | 4 p.m. | Fox | L.A. |
| 2 | Oct. 4 | 8 p.m. | FS1 | L.A. |
| 3 | Oct. 6 | 6 p.m. | FS1 | Atlanta |
| 4* | Oct. 7 | 6 p.m. | FS1 | Atlanta |
| 5* | Oct. 9 | 8 p.m. | Fox | L.A. |
*if necessary
What will the Dodgers' postseason lineup be?
The Dodgers finished the season shuffling their lineup depending on the handedness of the opposing starting pitcher, and it stands to reason that they will continue doing so in the postseason.
Here's how they could line up against right-handed pitchers:
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Will Smith, C
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Andy Pages, CF
- Tommy Edman, 2B
Shohei Ohtani has never hit in a batting order position other than leadoff in his MLB postseason career, but lately he has been hitting second against left-handers while Mookie Betts takes his old position atop the order.
Here's L.A.'s left-handed unit:
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Will Smith, C
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Andy Pages, CF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Tommy Edman, 2B
Both of those orders alternate left-right all the way down to Edman, a switch-hitter at the bottom. It's entirely possible the Dodgers go a different route, too.
What will the Dodgers' postseason rotation be?
That's fairly settled. The Dodgers will trot out the quartet of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. The order in which those arms are utilized remains to be seen, though the Dodgers have every reason to maximize innings for Yamamoto after what he did last year.
How has this season gone for the Dodgers?
It has gone well, by the standards of any other team.
By the standards of the Dodgers, well, there are a few dynamics at play. This is a good baseball team. They probably should've been better this season, and not just because they have the largest payroll in history, at a projected $410 million, per Roster Resource.
A two-time World Series champion filled its two biggest roster holes by giving two players, Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz, the highest salaries in the history of their positions. Entering the season, the Dodgers were estimated by the usually conservative PECOTA projections from Baseball Prospectus to win 104 games, and that didn't take into account acquiring a two-time reigning Cy Young Award winner in Skubal and more at the MLB trade deadline.
So in that sense, 100 wins is a disappointment. One of the most talented teams in MLB history (on paper at least) had more than its fair share of injuries, underperformances and mistakes. There was a point when the club seemed on the verge of letting the NL West become a race, as the Arizona Diamondbacks halved a division lead from 14 games to seven in the span of about a month between July and August, but then the D-backs got mired in their own slump and the Dodgers got hot again.
Overall, the Dodgers' issues boiled down to an offense that slumped hard in July and August, rough days for starting pitchers who will not be starting games in the playoffs and an epically bad bullpen night here and there. The first of those got better in September, though, which you can read more about here.
There is also the Dodgers' 38-37 record against teams with winning records this season, as their worst stretches of the year coincided with some of their toughest road trips and homestands, and that can leave an impression. Of course, it's a bit silly to worry about a team handling its business against good teams when it's going for a three-peat.
How does this team compare to last year's?
It's easy to remember the 2024 and 2025 Dodgers as juggernauts, but both of those teams had flaws that easily could've been fatal.
The 2024 Dodgers entered the postseason with a three-man rotation of Yamamoto, Walker Buehler and Jack Flaherty, with Clayton Kershaw, Glasnow, Dustin May, Gavin Stone, River Ryan and Emmet Sheehan among the starting pitchers on the injured list.
That team was so desperate for starting pitching help that it went full bullpen game while facing elimination at the hands of the Padres in the NLDS. It was only through the grace of a deep and competent bullpen that L.A. triumphed.
The 2025 team had the opposite problem. No one was doubting a rotation of Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow and Ohtani, but there were most certainly concerns about a bullpen whose late-inning arms consistently blew games well into September.
Once again, the Dodgers adjusted. With their rotation overflowing, they turned to a number of starting pitchers to fill the gaps. Every single pitcher who appeared in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series started at least nine games for this year's team.
With that in mind, the 2026 Dodgers might be the franchise's most balanced roster to enter the postseason in years, but there is once again a major question.
It's Ohtani. Let's get into that.
How's Shohei Ohtani doing?
Ohtani was the overwhelming NL MVP front-runner for the first half of this season, having begun the year as both a hitter and a pitcher for the first time in his Dodgers career.
Then Ohtani's knee started barking in July, resulting in the team taking him off the mound and giving him a lubricant injection during the All-Star break. He also developed a biceps issue at some point.
Those injuries didn't immediately stop Ohtani from playing. Much like he did in his recovery from internal brace surgery in 2024 and 2025, Ohtani played as the Dodgers' every-day designated hitter while rehabbing. However, the injuries clearly started to affect him in September, and the Dodgers opted to put him on the injured list for the first time in his tenure with the team.
Ohtani returned with five games left in the regular season and went 5-for-21 with 1 walk, 8 strikeouts and one extra-base hit, a double. Those numbers clearly aren't up to his standards, but if there's a reason for optimism, it's that he hit batted balls with exit velocities of 106.8, 106, 103.9 and 103.4 mph. He hadn't hit a ball that hard since August. Of course, the flip side of that optimism is maybe a 100% version of him would've hit them even harder.
Since his return, the Dodgers have insisted that Ohtani is feeling better, with hitting coach Aaron Bates saying Thursday that they had absolutely no concerns. The ship has sailed on Ohtani pitching again this season, though.
It still feels like Ohtani is the single biggest question for the Dodgers entering this postseason, given how long-term his knee issue has been. He at least got plenty of rest between his 15-day IL stint and the five days off between the end of the regular season and the start of the NLDS.
Do the Dodgers have a young, dynamic replacement at DH if Ohtani isn't healthy?
What an oddly specific question. The answer is yes, potentially.
It's not a stretch to say that Josue De Paula was the best hitting prospect in baseball at the time of his promotion to fill Ohtani's roster spot in September. At the time, every other position player in the MLB Pipeline top 10 was a shortstop who could offer significant two-way value, while De Paula will eventually be a bat-first corner outfielder at best and a bat-only first baseman at worst.
The good news is De Paula definitely looked like he belonged in his 11 games with the Dodgers while Ohtani was on the IL, slashing .323/.500/.581 and helping inject life into a previously struggling lineup. He was optioned when Ohtani came back, the timing of which made him available for the start of the NLDS.
In the playoffs, De Paula is likely to be the Dodgers' top left-handed bat off the bench, and he could fit in at designated hitter or corner outfield if someone gets hurt. It seems highly unlikely, however, that the Dodgers will take any plate appearances from Ohtani, barring a significant aggravation of that knee issue.
Are Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz still having horrifically bad debut seasons for the Dodgers?
Those two players were the butt of jokes all season after they signed record contracts to join the defending champions, then posted the worst seasons of their careers. However, both offered reason for optimism in September.
Tucker entered the month slashing .228/.326/.357 but finished the season at .262/.354/.536, numbers more in line with what the Dodgers were expecting when they signed him to a four-year, $240 million contract. His six homers in September were double what he had in any other month of the season.
In 2026, Díaz made seven appearances with a 10.50 ERA, spent three months on the injured list due to loose bodies in his elbow, came back for nine more appearances, posted a 12.91 ERA in those, then hit the IL one more time in August due to what was described as neck inflammation.
Then he came back in September and, like Tucker, performed like the player the Dodgers were initially expecting, with nine strikeouts and one hit allowed across five scoreless innings. Díaz no longer has the closer role, but he made as good a case as he could for late-inning work in October.
Tucker and Díaz still finished the year with horrendous numbers, and barring some postseason heroics, that's what most fans will remember. Still, it's important to know that the Dodgers might not treat them in October like their overall numbers would suggest.
How's the rest of the Dodgers' bullpen shaping up?
It's a diverse group. We've already talked about Díaz, who could be anything from middle reliever to closer by the end of the postseason. However, the current closer is Tanner Scott, who played the Díaz role last year as the high-priced reliever who struggled in his first year with the Dodgers.
Scott's second season in L.A. has gone far better. He converted 25 of 29 save attempts with a 2.69 ERA.
As for the other six spots in the bullpen, the contenders are Edgardo Henriquez, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Kris Bubic and Brock Stewart from the normal pot of relievers and Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Sheehan as overflow from the rotation.
Henriquez might be the most intriguing name from that group, as the flame-throwing right-hander was great during the regular season, only to hit the IL due to lower back discomfort in September. The Dodgers think he's trending toward playing in the NLDS.
Does a Dodgers World Series guarantee a salary cap?
You'd think. Some certainly seem to think. However, let's take a view rooted not in optimism but in realism.
The owners want a salary cap. They wanted one before Shohei Ohtani signed on the dotted line of a $700 million contract. They wanted one before Shohei Ohtani was born (what else happened in 1994?). They want a salary cap for the same reason every owner in sports has wanted a salary cap — not for competitive balance but to remove pressure on them to spend like they want to compete.
The Dodgers have made for a convenient boogeyman by being baseball's biggest spender and baseball's best team over the past several years. They must be stopped to save baseball, or so the argument goes, as no team is supposed to have L.A.'s combination of resources, competence and aggression. It's just not fair. It almost goes without saying in many discussions that the point of a salary cap is to end the Dodgers' unfair dynasty.
And yet, it really needs to be noted: Commissioner Rob Manfred does not fantasize about the Dodgers being forced to dismantle their tremendous machine — of Andrew Friedman, on his knees, begging a small-market team to take Glasnow's contract off his books — like some salary-cap proponents seem to do. Ohtani winning rings on the Dodgers has worked out quite nicely for baseball. A salary cap can be introduced for cost control and the veneer of parity, but MLB ultimately benefits from the large-market teams being contenders with the biggest stars. As such, it's hard to imagine a salary cap being introduced in such a way that the Dodgers, Yankees, Mets and other top spenders are forced to take immediate action to get below a line. A slow introduction of a cap or some sort of contract grandfathering seems far more likely, giving the Dodgers and others time to adjust.
The Dodgers' recent success isn't so much fuel for a salary cap as it is fuel for salary-cap opinions. It has certainly convinced many fans of a salary cap's necessity, but the MLBPA is playing cards at a different table. They don't want a salary cap, no matter what the Dodgers do, and they and the MLB owners are ultimately the people whose opinions matter here.
Limitations on the Dodgers would merely be a byproduct of MLB getting what it wants, and that would be completely antithetical to the history of the union. It's difficult to imagine the next month impacting salary-cap discussions to any significant degree.
What about the money problems with Dodgers ownership?
That's still in progress, and it remains unclear how much it will affect the Dodgers.
The short version of a very complicated story is that the companies operated by Dodgers majority owner Mark Walter were found to be doing business with one another at a rate much greater than what they were telling customers, investors and regulators. Walter is now facing considerable legal scrutiny and has reacted by selling whatever he can to pay off some of the loans that turned out to be less than kosher.
His biggest move was to sell his majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers at a franchise valuation of $12.5 billion, one year after buying the team at a $10 billion valuation. He has also offloaded his stake in the Premier League club Chelsea and the Ligue 1 club Strasbourg.
Those were big parts of Walter's sports portfolio, which also includes the WNBA's Los Angeles Sparks, the Cadillac Formula 1 team, the entire Professional Women's Hockey League and, of course, the Dodgers.
Dodgers leadership has repeatedly said the team isn't for sale. Of course, any sale would probably come out of nowhere — the Lakers' move was dropped on an otherwise uneventful Wednesday morning — but for now, that's mere speculation with the Dodgers.
One notable sign of trouble in Chavez Ravine, though, was a report that Walter recently approached Charter Communications about letting them out of their famously expensive Dodgers (and Lakers) contracts in exchange for a lump sum payout. It appears nothing has come out of that, but those are not stories you hear when everything is going well.
All of that's to say that Walter would likely welcome the immediate financial benefit of winning a third straight World Series even more than your typical billionaire. Of course, that outcome isn't up to him.

item.title: [Sportsnaut] Phillies Could Trade Kyle Schwarber This Winter? 5 Potential Destinations After New Speculation, Including the NY Yankees
item.dc:creator: Jasonburgosmma; Jason Burgos
item.description: After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a notable MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading star slugger Kyle Schwarber this winter. item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a notable MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading star slugger Kyle Schwarber this winter.
The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. While they didn’t win the National League East, the hope was that their talent-rich roster could still go on a deep run in the postseason. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts, Philadelphia came up short in their three-game Wild Card series against division rivals the Atlanta Braves.
Following their season-ending loss on Thursday, The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal claimed, “The Phillies at least need to kick around the idea of trading” the All-Star DH. A player the MLB insider feels doesn’t have an “oppressive” contract with four years and $120 million left on the deal.
While it is likely Schwarber is playing for the Phillies in 2027 and beyond, especially since he has a full no-trade clause, if the team did look to trade him this winter, here are five teams he could end up going to in the offseason.
Detroit Tigers
After trading top star Tarik Skubal before this season’s trade deadline, the Detroit Tigers will probably be open to diverting the money they were willing to give the reigning American League Cy Young to a different star.
While the Tigers are in greater need of elite pitching, adding one of the best sluggers in the game would be a massive addition for their lineup in 2027. Furthermore, after trading the two-time All-Star ace in the summer, they certainly now have the prospect assets that would interest the Phillies.
Toronto Blue Jays
This season was a massive disappointment for the Toronto Blue Jays. After being a couple of outs away from winning the World Series last fall, the Jays finished dead last in the AL East with a 79-83 record this year. So you can bet they will look to make a big move this offseason to get back into title contention in 2027.
If the Phillies actually make Schwarber available in trade talks, Toronto will be fascinated by the idea of pairing him with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. next season. The idea of Schwarber and Guerrero Jr. in the same batting order will give other AL East pitching staffs a cold sweat.
New York Yankees
The New York Yankees are still in the race to be champions in 2026. However, if they fall short of that yearly goal, the Yanks will surely look into adding a piece or two that can get them to end their 17-year title drought.
New York would need to find a new home for Giancarlo Stanton, but with only one guaranteed season for $15 million left on his deal, it may be possible this offseason. If they can trade the injury-prone five-time All-Star, Aaron Judge and Schwarber in the same lineup would be the most terrifying back-to-back in baseball.
Cincinnati Reds
To the surprise of many, the Cincinnati Reds were serious about bringing Schwarber back to his native Ohio this past offseason. And the 33-year-old was allegedly open to the idea as well. However, the draw of playing for a title contender he was familiar with and a huge contract brought him back to Philadelphia. The Reds would have some solid youngsters to offer in a trade, including top prospects that got the call to the big leagues this year.
Boston Red Sox
After a disappointing performance in the playoffs, it would not be a surprise if the Boston Red Sox looked to make a major move or two this winter. They don’t have an obvious DH for next season, so Schwarber would fill a clear need. Furthermore, slotting him into the middle of their batting order would make life far easier and offer more opportunities for Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, and Adley Rutschman to drive in runs.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers rotation is their greatest strength this October
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers won a championship in 2024 with a decimated starting rotation and dominant bullpen, then flipped the script with a stellar rotation buoying a shaky bullpen to win another title in 2025.
