item.content:encoded:
If only this month, root for the small-market Rays and Brewers. A World Series appearance by either or both might weaken the owners’ argument for a salary cap just enough to save next season. It wouldn’t hurt baseball, either, for Brewers long-limbed right-hander Jacob Misiorowski, he of the 100-plus mph delivery, the most strikeouts and a 1.80 ERA, to be featured on the biggest stage.
An extinct breed: If you’re wondering how many 20-game winners MLB has had this season, stop looking. There are none. Such is the state of the game.
Done and dusted: Just like that, the Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong, the presumptive NL MVP with 45 home runs and 41 stolen bases, is out of the playoffs after going hitless in two games against the Padres. That’s baseball.
Early services: Sunday’s Commanders-Colts from London is one of six 9:30 a.m. NFL starts from across the Atlantic in the next seven weeks. Far too many. It still is American football, isn’t it?
Disrespect: The Packers have been so listless this season that Fox moved their Nov. 11 game against the Bears from a late afternoon national window to 1 p.m. That’s a very early flex, but still leaves six nationally televised standalone Green Bay games on the schedule. Though not, the way things are going, for long.
No guarantees: The Rams, who some media magpies said could go undefeated, have already dropped two games in addition to losing quarterback sacker Myles Garrett for six weeks due to injury. The NFL is a cruel mistress.
An odd pairing: Nobody should ever underestimate the now 3-0 Chiefs. But a month ago, who could have imagined that the only Week 4 NFL game between unbeatens would include the Raiders?
In passing: This is my annual reminder that the Colts’ helmet is the best-looking helmet in football.
A team effort: Brian Schottenheimer apologized for mismanaging the end of the game against the Ravens, but the systemic blame for the Cowboys’ loss falls on Jerry Jones, who hired an inexperienced, first-time head coach who won’t cast much of a shadow over Jerry’s ego.
Idle thought: The most dangerous place to stand is between Jones and a TV camera.
Par for the course: The only thing the just completed Presidents Cup had in common with the last Ryder Cup were the scattered boorish shouts and chants from the American gallery.
For what it’s worth: It’s premature to assume the Protect College Sports Act will pass the House of Representatives. Or to think that the bill won’t introduce a new set of challenges and problems.
Roundball: NBA camps are open, and while most of the attention is on LeBron joining Philly, don’t sleep on the Heat now that Giannis Antetokounmpo has taken his talents to South Beach.
Great handle: A spectacular game against Alabama on Saturday would further boost the Heisman hopes of Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor, but the MSU player that catches my eye is running back Fluff Bothwell. He’s a cinch to make the All-Name Team.
Bob Molinaro is a former Virginian-Pilot sports columnist. His Weekly Briefing runs Fridays in The Pilot and Daily Press. He can be reached at bob5molinaro@gmail.com.

The *technically still* reigning AL Pennant winners failed to qualify for the MLB playoffs, and are officially in offseason mode. item.content:encoded:
There’s no sugarcoating that the Toronto Blue Jays had a rather disappointing 2026 season.
The *technically still* reigning AL Pennant winners failed to qualify for the MLB playoffs, and are officially in offseason mode.
Perhaps the biggest offseason storyline with the Blue Jays surrounds All-Star outfielder George Springer and his future in baseball.
There has been a lot of speculation about whether Springer will retire from the game of baseball, but that decision is likely not on the horizon until deeper into the MLB offseason.
However, Springer is on the record as being noncommittal about returning to MLB, as his contract has expired and he’s now a free agent.
More MLB on Heavy: Toronto Blue Jays Trade Prediction Lands 2X MLB All-Star Infielder
George Springer Noncommittal About MLB Future
Following the Toronto Blue Jays’ last regular-season contest, here was the message that George Springer sent to the media regarding his future:
“We’ll go into the offseason and I’ll see what happens….I’ll sit down with my wife at the end of this year and we’ll discuss whatever’s going to happen. But I love my family and if that requires me to be with them, I’ll be with them.”
It’s a fair sentiment to make, as Springer needs some time to weigh the massive life decision and what could potentially lie ahead for his career and future.
MLBTR.com’s Mark Polishuk added (about the Springer speculation):
“While he’ll surely draw interest in free agency, Springer’s market will be limited as a 37-year-old who is essentially a DH-only player at this stage of his career. With 13 seasons played, four All-Star nods, almost $200MM in career earnings, and a World Series ring (and a World Series MVP trophy) with the 2017 Astros on his resume, this may be enough for Springer to call it a career and spend more time with his wife and three young sons.”
George Springer is an extremely accomplished MLB player, but after a long list of nagging injuries throughout his career, it makes sense why he doesn’t want to subject himself to that discomfort any longer.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Mets Tasked with 9 Free Agency Decisions This Offseason
If George Springer’s MLB Career Is Over… It Was a Good One…
George Springer has played in MLB for the past 13 seasons (playing with just two organizations).
Across 1571 total games played, Springer carries a lifetime batting average of .265 with 308 home runs, 850 RBI, and 1595 career hits.
Looking at his Baseball-Reference page, it’s hard to see a major statistical hitting category that Springer would like to reach a milestone in.
After a considerable drop in production in 2026, it’s also unclear if the Blue Jays would even want to retain the 37-year-old All-Star, which brings up the idea that Springer may just want to call it quits rather than play for another organization at this juncture in his career.
Either way, his status is still up in the air, but it will be a big storyline to follow this entire offseason.

item.content:encoded:
October baseball is upon us, and we have a massive playoff game on Thursday night.
The Philadelphia Phillies and Atlanta Braves are the only teams remaining in the wild card round, setting up a standalone Game 3 on Thursday night.
The Phillies came back from a 3-1 deficit in Game 2 – after a key Bryce Harper error – to win in extra innings behind solo shots from Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Alec Bohm.
The starting pitching matchup for Game 3 is murky at the moment, although two beat reporters gave some insight into what these teams might do.
Long-time Phillies reporter Jim Salisbury shared that he’s hearing veteran Aaron Nola will get the start for the Phillies while the Braves will go with an opener in Ray Kerr. The Atlanta bullpen is elite, ranking fourth in MLB in ERA during the regular season.
Braves beat reporter Mark Bowman also shared some insight to the starting pitching matchup, mentioning that Braves righty Grant Holmes could be used as the “bulk” option behind Kerr on Thursday. He also believes the Phillies will use a combo of Nola and ace Zack Wheeler, who would be pitching on short rest after leading the Phillies to a win on Sunday.
All hands are going to be on deck in this matchup for both teams, as this is a win-or-go-home scenario.
Oddsmakers have set the Phillies as slight favorites on the road, a sign that they have more confidence in Philly’s options to start in this game.
Here’s a breakdown of the odds, a player prop to bet and my prediction for Thursday’s Game 3.
Phillies vs. Braves Odds, Run Line and Total
Run Line
- Phillies -1.5 (+144)
- Braves +1.5 (-174)
Moneyline
- Phillies: -118
- Braves: -102
Total
- 7.5 (Over +100/Under -120)
Phillies vs. Braves Probable Pitchers
- Philadelphia: TBA
- Atlanta: TBA
Phillies vs. Braves How to Watch
- Date: Thursday, Oct. 1
- Time: 8:00 p.m. EST
- Venue: Truist Park
- How to Watch (TV): NBC, Peacock
- Series: Tied 1-1
Phillies vs. Braves Best MLB Prop bets
Braves Best MLB Prop Bet
- Drake Baldwin OVER 1.5 Hits, Runs, RBIs (-108)
In today’s edition of Walk-Off Wagers – our MLB Best Bets column at SI – I shared why Baldwin is worth a look if Nola gets the start:
If Nola ends up getting the start, it’s a good sign for Braves catcher/designated hitter Drake Baldwin.
Baldwin picked up two hits and a run batted in on Wednesday, and he’s fared extremely well against Nola in his career.
The 25-year-old is 5-for-11 (.455) against Nola in his career, with a .955 OPS. He’s driven in one run against the Phillies veteran, and Nola has struggled quite a bit with the long ball this season, allowing 37 in 33 starts during the regular season.
A homer would immediately hit this prop for Baldwin, and he’s coming off a strong showing on Wednesday. During the regular season, the Braves star hit .284 overall and .307 against right-handed pitching.
Baldwin also entered the playoffs on a hot streak, batting .360 with two home runs, five runs batted in and a .951 OPS over the final two weeks (12 games). He’s a pretty interesting bet with this prop set at -108 on Thursday.
Phillies vs. Braves Prediction and Pick
Another play from today’s Walk-Off Wagers, I’m going to back the Phillies to win and advance after stealing Game 2:
There’s certainly an argument to be made for the Braves, who went 23 games over .500 at home in the regular season, but I lean with the Phillies in Game 3.
If Wheeler is able to pitch on short rest in any capacity, he’ll be by far the best pitcher in this game and had a massive finish to the regular season. Wheeler had a 1.71 ERA in September, lowering his season-long ERA to 3.00. He may not be able to give the Phils a ton of length, but it should help ease the pressure on their bullpen.
Nola has pitched in a ton of big games in his career, and I don’t want to downplay his two solid starts against Atlanta earlier this month. In two outings, Nola allowed just 10 hits and three earned runs across 13.1 innings of work.
The Braves have only used Kerr as an opener once this season, and Holmes had some very shaky advanced numbers in the regular season, ranking in the 12th percentile in expected ERA and the 18th percentile in expected BAA.
The Atlanta bullpen has been taxed in this series, pitching Didier Fuentes, Dylan Lee and Rasiel Iglesias in back-to-back days. That’s not nothing. Can the Atlanta ‘pen hold up after blowing Game 2?
I’d much rather take the Phillies and their proven veteran starters in a winner-take-all game, especially after they showed they can power themselves to a win on Wednesday.
Pick: Phillies Moneyline (-118 at DraftKings)

item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing 93-loss season, Royals president of baseball operations J.J. Picollo said the team plans to be “aggressive in acquisitions.” But that aggressiveness, he cautioned, should not be confused with a willingness to spend aggressively on the payroll. He addressed the media along with manager Matt Quatraro in the team’s annual end-of-year press conference on Wednesday.
The season did not go as planned, with the team stumbling to a 12-19 start by the end of April. Picollo took addressed the slow start by saying “we’re responsible for the performance in April and May.” He did point out the World Baseball Classic kept some Royals players away from the team during spring training, making it more difficult to build team camaraderie. And injuries made it difficult for the team to climb their way out of the hole they had dug.
“We weren’t very good in April, and we weren’t very good in the beginning of May. I can’t sit here and tell you that I know we would have been good in June, July, August, and September, but if we had had those players on our roster and healthy and available, I think we could have made a better run.”
The Royals lost key players like Maikel Garcia and Vinnie Pasquantino early in the year, in addition to having their pitching staff decimated by injuries over the summer. The Royals announced changes to their medical staff, although Picollo denied the injuries were the reason for the moves. He also contended that despite all the adversity, the team has to win.
“That being said, nobody feels sorry for you. You got to go out and win.”
Here is what Picollo had to say about how he plans to address team needs this offseason.
The bullpen
”The bullpen is going to be a focus for us,” said Picollo. “There’s no question.”
Royals relievers had a 5.07 ERA, second-worst in baseball, and a league-worst 6.65 ERA in the ninth inning. The team lost closer Carlos Estévez to injury after his first game, and got disappointing performances from Lucas Erceg and Matt Strahm.
While Picollo expects the team to be aggressive, he added “I don’t want that mistaken for aggressive payroll spending.” He noted that the team was top five in spending on the bullpen over the last three years, but that spending on relievers may not be the solution due to the volatility of their performance.
“We have to look into ways at being more efficient,” he said, adding that they tried to look for that “diamond in the rough” late this year with waiver claims and small deals. They sought pitchers that presented different arm angles and pitches to give hitters varying looks.
“There’s not a clear, definitive answer on how to pull put a bullpen together. But I think the variety of ‘different looks,’ ‘different stuff’ type of relievers is the way we’re probably going to go.”
Back in August, owner John Sherman said he thought the bullpen could be “cobbled” together without spending too much money.
While Picollo highlighted the pitching of Steven Cruz and Nate Pearson down the stretch, the 2027 closer may not be on the roster right now.
“I don’t know if we’ll be able to sit here today and tell you we’ll have a closer. Internally, we don’t think we necessarily have it.”
Daniel Lynch IV, who enjoyed a breakthrough season in the bullpen, will be given a chance to compete for a starting spot next year. Lynch had a 1.96 ERA in 46 relief appearances this year, and a 6.53 ERA in 10 starts.
Starting pitching
Picollo said starting depth was their biggest priority after upgrading the bullpen. He admitted that the starting pitching depth he had amassed before the season was not nearly enough.
“It was as confident as I’ve ever been in starting pitching depth,” he said before discussing the injuries that hit the pitching staff. Cole Ragans, Kris Bubic, Ryan Bergert, and Stephen Kolek all missed significant time this season.
“So we’re never going to take starting pitching for granted.”
Next year’s rotation will feature Michael Wacha, Seth Lugo, and Noah Cameron, but the team will have to figure out who will fill the last two spots. The team expects to pick up the option of Tony Gonsolin, the former Dodgers All-Star pitcher who was signed late in the year and pitched in one game for the Royals. He could compete for a rotation spot along with Lynch, and Randy Dobnak, who impressed with a 3.51 ERA in 15 games.
Offense
As far as the offense, Picollo liked some of the underlying things they did, but ultimately the team did not score enough runs, particularly on the road. The Royals averaged 4.26 runs per game overall, finishing 21st in baseball. That was a slight improvement over their performance in 2025 when they scored 4.02 runs per game, 26th in baseball. But they finished dead last in baseball in runs on the road, averaging just 3.62 per game.
“It’s a combination of things. It’s getting on base at a greater clip. It’s running the bases well. It’s putting the ball in play when you need to with a man in scoring position. A lot is made of batting average with runners in scoring position - for us its more about ‘did you get him in?’”
He confirmed Ken Rosenthal’s report from Tuesday that hitting coach Alec Zumwalt has been reassigned to focus more on minor league development, but Picollo clarified that this was not a reflection of performance, and had been the plan all along. Zumwalt had worked with the current core of Royals hitters in the minors, and had ascended to the big league level with them. The team wants him back working with young minor league hitters, while assistant hitting coaches Marcus Thames and Connor Dawson work with the big league hitters. The Royals will likely hire another assistant hitting coach, but Picollo backed the work of Zumwalt.
“We’re not disappointed with his performance. We think he’s a very good hitting coach.”
The team will look for offensive upgrades in the outfield. Picollo noted the outfield defense regressed this season, despite the fences at Kauffman Stadium being moved in leaving less room to cover. Outfield prospect Carson Roccaforte could be in the mix, although he is left-handed and Picollo noted that the team is already very left-handed heavy.
The team will be “open to any and all ideas” on trades, even if that means trading players on the roster. Picollo added he is not interested in trading players for prospects, given their timeline and expectations to contend.
“We need to add players that help us at the major league level.”
Spending
Picollo said he does not have a specific payroll figure, but noted that ownership has approved additional spending when he has brought forward opportunities worth pursuing.
“I’ve always felt like it’s not my job to worry about the payroll. Our job is to get the most out of whatever we have,” said Picollo, noting there are teams in the playoffs with lower payrolls than the Royals, while many teams that spent a lot are sitting at home.
“I don’t think payroll is indicative of success on the field. I think success on the field comes with knowing your roster and how to get the most out of your roster and that’s our task. That’s what we need to do.”
Sherman said in August that the team is “freeing up some money” the team could invest, with about $30 million expected to come off the payroll with impending free agents.
When asked about potential long-term contracts for Jac Caglianone or Carter Jensen, Picollo deferred, saying that they typically don’t seriously consider such deals until after a player’s second year of service time. Both players just completed their first full season in the big leagues, finishing strong with each hitting over 20 home runs and posting an OPS+ over 120.
The Royals may have to work quickly to address their shortcomings simply because of the looming potential work stoppage. The collective bargaining agreement expires on December 1, which could lead to an end to free agent signings until a new labor deal is worked out.
“The aggressiveness in November is going to be important for us, as we expect the entire industry to be fairly busy.”
But it is clear the Royals have a lot do before the next season begins. The Royals entered 2026 expecting to build on back-to-back winning seasons. Instead, they finished with the fifth-worst record in baseball and now face significant questions in the bullpen, starting rotation and outfield. Picollo acknowledged that the fans demand more.
“It’s refreshing to know that our fans have high expectations. We want them to have high expectations, because we gave them reason to have high expectations,” said Picollo.
“With that comes to responsibility of getting it done. I think we feel pressure every year to win.”

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff schedule 2026: Full bracket, scores, times, TV channels to watch every postseason series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
More than seven months after pitchers and catchers reported to spring training, it's time to determine which team will wear the MLB crown in 2026.
Twelve teams reached the postseason bracket, and any discussion about favorites has to start with the two-time defending champion Dodgers. Los Angeles wasn't necessarily dominant during the regular season and enters October with concerns about the health of the planet's best player, Shohei Ohtani, but it has proven unwise to bet against LA lately.
While the Dodgers are in the midst of a dynastic run, neither of the teams that owned the best records in their respective leagues during the regular season — the Brewers and Rays — has won a World Series. Victory would be particularly sweet for either of those fan bases, along with the other postseason entrant without a title, the Padres.
Who will survive the gauntlet to lift the Commissioner's Trophy at the end of October? Here's when and where to watch every game.
Where to watch MLB playoffs 2026
- TV channels: Fox, FS1, TBS, NBC, NBCSN
The 2026 MLB postseason will have a new look for the opening round, with NBC carrying every wild card game on its platforms: NBC, NBCSN and/or Peacock.
After that, the familiar rotation returns. This year's NL playoffs will air on Fox or FS1 while the AL will be on TBS, with the World Series set to air on Fox as it has every year since 2000.
Fans can stream every postseason game except Peacock exclusives with DIRECTV, which offers a free trial to new subscribers.
All games airing on NBC, NBCSN, Fox and FS1 can be streamed with fubo, which also offers a free trial.

item.title: [Sportsnaut] Red Sox Paid a Massive Price for Adley Rutschman to Win in October. Then They Went 0-2
item.dc:creator: Gary Adornato
item.description: Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October. Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman. They didn’t need him to save their season. They didn’t need him to drag them into postseason contention. item.content:encoded:
Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October.
Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman.
They didn’t need him to save their season.
They didn’t need him to drag them into postseason contention.
And they certainly didn’t surrender four prospects and their starting major-league catcher simply to hang a Wild Card banner.
Boston was already one of baseball’s hottest teams when it acquired Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles at the Aug. 3 trade deadline. The Red Sox had transformed their season with a remarkable summer surge and were firmly positioned to reach the postseason.
Rutschman was supposed to provide something more.
October.
The Red Sox paid an enormous price to a division rival because they believed adding a three-time All-Star catcher could help turn a playoff team into a championship team.
Instead, their postseason lasted two games.
The New York Yankees completed an embarrassing two-game sweep Wednesday night, beating Boston 9-2 after a 9-0 demolition in Game 1.
Final aggregate score: Yankees 18, Red Sox 2.
Boston managed only seven hits in 18 innings and batted .117 in the series. The Yankees did all of it without three-time American League MVP Aaron Judge, who was sidelined by a calf injury.
And Rutschman?
The expensive deadline addition Boston acquired specifically to make a difference at this time of year couldn’t make one.
Making matters considerably worse, the Yankees reportedly had their own opportunity to acquire Rutschman.
They decided Baltimore’s price was too high.
Then they sent Boston home.
Boston Didn’t Need Adley Rutschman to Reach the Playoffs
This is the most important context when evaluating the trade.
The Red Sox weren’t desperately chasing the final Wild Card position when chief baseball officer Craig Breslow made the deal.
Boston had gone 23-3 beginning July 2, establishing itself as one of baseball’s hottest teams and putting itself firmly on a postseason trajectory before Rutschman ever put on a Red Sox uniform.
That’s why simply pointing out that Boston reached the postseason after acquiring him misses the point.
Reaching October wasn’t supposed to justify the trade.
Winning in October was.
The Red Sox ultimately finished 87-75 and secured a Wild Card berth. Then the Yankees eliminated them in two games.
So what exactly did Boston’s massive deadline investment change?
Not its playoff destination and certainly not its playoff result.
Adley Rutschman Didn’t Deliver When Boston Needed Him Most
This was the stage for which Boston acquired Rutschman.
Instead, the Red Sox scored two runs in two games.
Rutschman finished the series 1-for-8 with three strikeouts and did not drive in a run as Boston’s offense was overwhelmed by Cam Schlittler and Max Fried.
And one of his most consequential moments came defensively during Boston’s disastrous sixth inning Wednesday.
With the Red Sox trailing 2-1 and desperately trying to keep their season alive, Spencer Jones reached first after swinging at a third strike from Garrett Crochet that got away from Rutschman.
Jones then stole second and advanced to third when Rutschman’s throw sailed into center field.
George Lombard Jr. followed with an RBI single.
The inning disintegrated from there.
By the time Boston finally recorded the third out, New York had scored six runs and transformed a one-run elimination game into another rout.
It would be ridiculous to blame Rutschman for Boston’s elimination. The Red Sox were comprehensively outplayed, their offense disappeared and their pitching couldn’t contain New York when the series was on the line.
But that’s precisely why the trade deserves scrutiny.
Boston didn’t surrender a collection of valuable young players for another complementary piece.
It paid for a difference-maker.
When the difference needed to be made, it wasn’t.
Look at What Boston Gave Baltimore
The price looks even more jarring now.
Baltimore received five players:
RHP Anthony Eyanson: Boston’s No. 2 prospect at the time of the trade and a top-50 prospect in baseball. He immediately became Baltimore’s top-ranked prospect.
RHP Kyson Witherspoon: Another highly regarded pitching prospect who immediately became one of the better prospects in Baltimore’s system.
OF Enddy Azocar: A promising young outfielder who added another high-upside asset to Baltimore’s farm system.
C Carlos Narváez: Boston’s starting major-league catcher, giving Baltimore an immediate replacement behind the plate.
OF Harold Rivas: The 18-year-old outfielder eventually sent to Baltimore as the player to be named later.
Boston received Rutschman, catcher Jake Rogers and cash.
Four prospects and a starting major-league catcher.
Sent directly to an American League East rival.
That’s not a routine deadline upgrade.
That’s a significant transfer of organizational value made specifically because Boston believed Rutschman could help it win immediately.
The immediate payoff?
Thirty-two regular-season games and a postseason that lasted two losses.
The Yankees Were Offered Adley Rutschman, Too. They Walked Away.
This is where Boston’s decision becomes even harder to swallow.
The Red Sox weren’t the only AL East contender that discussed Rutschman with Baltimore.
The Yankees reportedly explored acquiring him before the deadline.
According to the New York Post, Baltimore’s asking price from New York included pitching prospect Elmer Rodríguez, catcher Austin Wells, outfield prospect Yostin Pena and either Will Warren or Ryan Weathers.
The Yankees decided it was too much.
Boston decided its own massive prospect package wasn’t.
Two months later, the teams met in October.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox.
That alone doesn’t prove New York made the correct long-term decision. Prospects fail. Rutschman could return to All-Star form. The careers of the players Boston and New York retained or surrendered will ultimately determine how these decisions age.
But the immediate comparison couldn’t be much uglier for Breslow.
New York kept its catcher.
It kept its prospects.
It kept its young pitching.
And it eliminated the team that paid Baltimore’s price.
Ben Rice Made the Comparison Even More Painful
There is another piece of this that Boston probably doesn’t want to think about.
The Yankees didn’t merely decline to acquire Rutschman.
They watched one of their own young players become the kind of offensive weapon Boston hoped it was acquiring.
Ben Rice erupted for 41 home runs during the regular season.
Then he opened the postseason by destroying the Red Sox.
Rice went 4-for-5 with two home runs and six RBIs in New York’s 9-0 Game 1 victory.
Six RBIs.
Boston scored two runs in the entire series.
The Yankees didn’t need to surrender a massive package to Baltimore to find an impact bat.
They developed one.
Boston went shopping for an established star.
Then Rice helped send its expensive new catcher and the rest of the Red Sox home.
Boston Didn’t Even Get the Superstar Version of Rutschman
Boston can at least point to Rutschman’s impressive résumé.
He was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2019 MLB Draft, became the centerpiece of Baltimore’s rebuild and developed into one of baseball’s most recognizable catchers.
But the Red Sox weren’t trading for his résumé.
They were trading for what he could do in 2026 and 2027.
That’s an important distinction.
Rutschman was already on the injured list with wrist inflammation when Boston acquired him.
Once healthy, he played 32 regular-season games for the Red Sox and hit .222 with a .278 on-base percentage and .410 slugging percentage.
His OPS was .688.
He hit five home runs and drove in 13 runs.
His 92 OPS+ meant he was eight percent below league average offensively after adjusting for league and ballpark conditions.
Boston surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for an immediate upgrade and received below-average regular-season offense.
Then came October.
No transformational performance.
No postseason victory.
No series win.
Craig Breslow Made a Win-Now Trade. Boston Didn’t Win.
There is nothing inherently wrong with trading prospects.
Contending organizations sometimes become too protective of players who have never taken a major-league at-bat. Windows close. Players get hurt. Rosters change.
When an organization has an opportunity to win a championship, there are times when being aggressive is exactly the right approach.
But here’s the other side of that philosophy:
If you’re going to make a win-now trade, eventually you have to win now.
Breslow pushed a significant portion of Boston’s prospect capital into the middle of the table.
The Red Sox responded by finishing 87-75.
Then they arrived at Yankee Stadium and were outscored 18-2 in two games.
That’s not an October run.
That’s barely an October appearance.
The Yankees advanced. Boston went home before October was two days old.
And the player Breslow acquired as his blockbuster deadline upgrade produced neither the offensive impact nor the postseason difference Boston was paying for.
Meanwhile, Baltimore Gets to Keep All Five Players
This is the part that could hurt Boston considerably longer than Wednesday night’s loss.
Baltimore doesn’t need all four prospects to become stars for this trade to sting the Red Sox.
It doesn’t even need two of them to become stars.
If Eyanson develops into a quality major-league starter, or Witherspoon reaches his upside, or Azocar or Rivas eventually develops into an everyday player, Boston could spend years watching a division rival benefit from its deadline gamble.
Narváez is already a major-league catcher.
The Orioles essentially converted one player approaching his final season of club control into five assets.
Boston acquired the short-term star.
Baltimore acquired years of potential value.
And the Orioles didn’t have to wait long to see the first part of their gamble work.
Rutschman’s first postseason with Boston lasted two games.
Now Boston May Have to Pay for Rutschman Again
That’s what makes this more than simply a failed 2026 deadline gamble.
Rutschman can become a free agent after the 2027 season.
Boston therefore has another major decision coming.
The Red Sox can attempt to sign him to a lucrative extension, committing significant long-term money to a catcher whose offensive production has declined from his early-career peak and who has dealt with injuries.
They can let him play out 2027 and risk watching him depart as a free agent roughly 17 months after surrendering four prospects and Narváez to acquire him.
Or they can eventually trade him and attempt to recover some of the organizational value they sent Baltimore.
None looks particularly attractive this morning.
And Boston should be especially careful about allowing the enormous acquisition cost to influence its next decision.
The prospects are gone regardless.
Paying Rutschman a huge extension because Boston already paid dearly to acquire him would be classic sunk-cost thinking.
The next decision has to be based on what Rutschman is likely to provide going forward, not what Boston surrendered to get him.
He could make this entire discussion look foolish next season. Rutschman is talented enough to rebound, produce another All-Star season and become an important part of a championship contender.
But that’s a 2027 argument.
We know what happened in 2026.
Boston was already headed toward the postseason.
Baltimore put an enormous price on Rutschman.
The Yankees looked at that price and walked away.
The Red Sox paid it.
Then those two teams met in October.
New York outscored Boston 18-2, swept the Red Sox in two games and advanced without Aaron Judge.
Boston went home.
And Baltimore still has all five players.

item.title: [mlb.com] Houston? No problem! White Sox end 21-year wait with sweep
item.dc:creator: Scott Merkin
item.description: HOUSTON -- There was a moment with nobody out in the sixth inning Wednesday night during Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series that perfectly encapsulated the White Sox remarkable season and the downright fun they’ve had along the way. item.content:encoded:
HOUSTON -- There was a moment with nobody out in the sixth inning Wednesday night during Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series that perfectly encapsulated the White Sox remarkable season and the downright fun they’ve had along the way.
Chase Meidroth connected on a three-run home run off Bryan Abreu, turning a one-run lead into a 7-3 advantage, which was ultimately the final score. But it was Meidroth’s reaction that reinforced the point.
Meidroth pumped his fist and screamed with joy from the moment he connected until he touched home plate, his emotions on full display. Back in the visitors’ clubhouse, the champagne was chilling as the White Sox prepared to take another somewhat unexpected step in the postseason.
“When I’m locked in on the field, I don’t know what goes through my mind,” Meidroth said. “All I’m thinking about is me and the baseball and trying to compete. But I had a good feeling.”
Good feelings have surrounded the White Sox since Spring Training, even dating back to SoxFest in late January. They’ve arguably been baseball’s best story in 2026, and perhaps one of the best in sports.
But this two-game sweep against the undermanned Astros proved they are a talented team to be reckoned with throughout the postseason. They are more than the young, energetic squad that shook off three consecutive 100-plus-loss campaigns to reach the playoffs.
Their second clubhouse celebration in a week -- and one of five they hope to have this postseason -- marked their first playoff series victory since 2005. That last series victory was a four-game sweep over the Astros in the World Series, with Games 3 and 4 played at what is now Daikin Park.
“These players are scared of nothing,” White Sox general manager Chris Getz said. “And whether it be myself or others, it’s like, 'How do we continue to nurture and fuel this group?'”
"We were able to do that with two games that I thought were emblematic of how we've won all season,” manager Will Venable said. “Contributions from everywhere. Sammy [Antonacci] setting the tone, great job down the lineup with everyone behind him. Guys pitching in different spots, going out whenever and getting the job done, and they did it."
For the second straight game, Chicago took control in the first inning with the help of Houston's poor defense. The White Sox scored four runs off Astros ace Hunter Brown, who had a 6-0 record with a 2.39 ERA over six career starts against the White Sox entering Wednesday.
Antonacci doubled on a line drive to left field that Yordan Alvarez seemed to have a play on but didn’t make. Kyle Teel singled home Antonacci, and Miguel Vargas reached on third baseman Nick Allen’s fielding error.
Andrew Benintendi singled home a second run, and when Lucas Spence's throw home got away from catcher Yainer Diaz, Vargas scored the third run. Tristan Peters then added an RBI single to cap the scoring in the opening frame.
Houston crept back with solo home runs from Jeremy Peña, Cam Smith and Jose Altuve off White Sox ace Sean Burke, who struck out eight over four innings. The Astros had a golden opportunity in the fifth inning, putting runners on first and second with one out for Alvarez. Anthony Kay was on the mound for his first true relief appearance this season.
Kay fell behind in the count, 3-0, threw a pitch in the zone that was taken by Alvarez and then got him to fly out to Antonacci in left on the next pitch. Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases, but Altuve flied out to right to end the frame.
Then Meidroth provided breathing room in the sixth, launching his three-run homer to restore Chicago’s four-run lead. Twelve outs stood between the White Sox and playoff history, but they had reasserted control, and Erick Fedde handled the final two innings to finish it off.
“You saw how it was this series,” Kay said. “Everyone didn't worry about themselves, just played as a team and did the best they could.”
“Hard to imagine myself in that situation, honestly, but I'm so glad they chose me with the ball and to give the team the win,” Fedde said. “This whole fan base deserved [this]. This whole organization deserved [this]. Feels good to move on to the next round.”
And now, it’s on to Cleveland and the AL Division Series for the White Sox, in the ongoing saga between AL Central rivals. The White Sox won the season series, 7-6, but the Guardians won the division by one game to earn home-field advantage.
Cleveland features a strong rotation and one of the best closers in the game in Cade Smith. Then again, the Guardians will see a team on a roll that has been 21 years in the making.

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO (AP) — The Chicago team that didn't have the pope on its side is heading meekly into the offseason.
Pete Crow-Armstrong and the Chicago Cubs came out to sunny San Diego and wilted like a tourist without enough sunscreen, swept out of the National League Wild Card Series by a San Diego Padres team eager for redemption and perhaps primed for a deep postseason run.
The Cubs lost 4-1 in Game 2 on Wednesday night at Petco Park to exit the postseason. They came in with the highest-scoring offense in the majors and head home having scored only one run on eight hits.
They were ushered out by the Reaper himself, San Diego's All-Star fireballing closer Mason Miller who allowed Nico Hoerner's one-out double — the Cubs' only extra-base hit in the two games — before getting Carson Kelly to ground out to shortstop to end it. The No. 4-seeded Padres move on to face the NL Central champion and top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers in an NL Division Series.
The loss by the fifth-seeded Cubs came several hours after the Chicago White Sox, who received a letter of support from lifelong fan Pope Leo XIV, swept the Houston Astros in Game two of an AL Wild Card Series.
The Cubs beat the Padres 2-1 in a Wild Card Series last fall at Wrigley Field.
Several Cubs players lingered along the dugout rail watching the Padres and their yellow towel-waving fans celebrate on a 69-degree night.
Players hugged inside the quiet clubhouse.
Crow-Armstrong, the frontrunner for NL MVP after becoming the first Cubs player to post a 40-40 season, struggled to find perspective while placing blame on himself.
"None of it feels good," Crow-Armstrong said. "That's it. So I'm just feeling pretty disappointed in myself, but that's for me to work on."
Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman, the Cubs' 1-2 hitters, combined to go 0 for 15 with one walk and eight strikeouts. Crow-Armstrong had the walk in Game 1. Each of them struck out three times in Game 1 while Crow-Armstrong had a walk.
Asked how he'd process his performance, Crow-Armstrong said: "That's not really for me to answer right now. I mean, yeah, you can look at the scoreboard, you can look at the stat sheet, wherever you get your numbers from, and it is clear to see that I didn't contribute. So, that's not for me to feel about right now. I wouldn't process that well if I was."
The Southern California native, who had 45 homers and 41 stolen bases, said the Cubs "showed a lot of heart and a lot of fight through all the challenge. But I mean, I would say to start, like, I show up. I show up when it matters in these games, you know? I think that would help us immediately, but that's all I got right now."
The Cubs dominated the season series 5-1. The teams hadn't seen each other since July 1, when the Cubs handed the Padres their worst loss ever, 23-3 at Wrigley Field as they hit eight home runs.
"The San Diego group, they threw the ball really well," Dansby Swanson said. "They didn't miss spots often, and if they did miss, it was in good locations. It's a really talented staff. They game-planned for us really well and we weren't able to get traction. We gave ourselves a couple of chances here and there, but, we weren't able to capitalize and keep anything going."
Said manager Craig Counsell: "You've just got to go play well and win games. In the end, we're walking away unfulfilled and disappointed."
___

item.content:encoded:
HOUSTON -- Chase Meidroth hit a backbreaking three-run home run in the sixth inning to help the Chicago White Sox make a big early lead stand up in a 7-3 victory Wednesday against the Houston Astros that capped a two-game sweep of their American League wild-card series.
The White Sox earned their first postseason series victory since their sweep of the Astros in the 2005 World Series. The White Sox will face the Cleveland Guardians in a best-of-5 American League Division Series that begins Saturday in Cleveland.
“I’m really just happy for everybody over the last few years who experienced White Sox baseball when it obviously wasn’t at its best,” Chicago manager Will Venable said postgame. “It’s such a storied franchise. (White Sox owner) Jerry (Reinsdorf) put so much into this team, loves this team so much, and to be able to reward him and the city of Chicago, who have been in our corner and supported us from Day 1 that I’ve been there, just feels really good.
“I’m proud of the guys and certainly happy for them. They’re probably the only ones in this country that believed they could be in this spot, and they maintained that belief in the beginning of the season and went throughout the season maintaining that. They made it happen.”
The Astros returned to the playoffs after a one-year absence but have not advanced past the wild-card round since 2023.
“(Astros owner) Jim (Crane) has been very clear about his process and when he wants to have that conversation,” Houston manager Joe Espada, who finishes the season without an extension in place to stay with the Astros. “I respect the process and how blessed I’ve been to have been here for over nine years, experienced so many division titles, championship series, World Series -- winning one as a bench coach. As a manager, I have witnessed so many great moments. Obviously, I would like to continue enjoying those moments.”
After the Astros left the bases loaded in the fifth, Meidroth extended a 4-3 lead by driving a 3-1 slider from Astros reliever Bryan Abreu 390 feet to left-center field.
The White Sox scored four runs in the top of the first inning off Astros ace Hunter Brown (0-1), who didn’t make it out of the first as he allowed five hits, four runs (three earned) and one walk while the defense contributed two errors.
Kyle Teel, Andrew Benintendi and Tristan Peters recorded RBI singles in the first while Miguel Vargas reached on a fielding error by Astros third baseman Nick Allen and scored on a throwing error by center fielder Lucas Spence. Brown retired two of the nine batters he faced.
The Astros began a methodical climb back into the game in the bottom of the first when leadoff man Jeremy Pena smacked the first of three solo home runs off Chicago starter Sean Burke.
Pena drilled a 1-1 slider 395 feet to left-center field. An inning later, Cam Smith bashed a 1-0 sinker 440 feet to left field to close the margin to 4-2. In the fourth inning, Jose Altuve socked his 28th career postseason homer -- second all-time to Manny Ramirez -- to left to bring Houston within 4-3.
Burke allowed three runs and four hits while recording eight strikeouts in four innings. When the Astros built another serious threat in the fifth, White Sox left-hander Anthony Kay delivered.
After reliever Huascar Brazoban hit Cam Smith with a pitch and gave up a single to Pena, Kay (1-0) entered with one out and retired MVP candidate Yordan Alvarez on a deep fly just in front of the Crawford Boxes in left. Kay loaded the bases by walking Isaac Paredes but induced Altuve into a harmless flyout to right to end the inning.
Peter Lambert, the Astros’ third pitcher of the game, needed only 36 pitches to work three perfect innings, but he walked Benintendi and Peters to open the sixth. After Abreu entered the game, Meidroth faked a bunt that enabled pinch runner Luisangel Acuna and Peters to steal third and second base, respectively. With the infield in, Meidroth made it moot by crushing a hanging slider he immediately knew was a home run.

The Chicago Cubs are in the middle of a National League Wild Card Series against the San Diego Padres at Petco Park.
The Padres won the first game of the series 8-0 on Tuesday. Game 2 is scheduled to begin at 9:00 p.m. CDT on Wednesday.
If the Padres win tonight, the Cubs will be eliminated from the playoffs. If the Cubs win, there will be a Game 3 tomorrow. The winner of the series will play the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Division Series.
Before Wednesday night’s game, Cubs shortstop Dansby Swanson made an honest statement.
Chicago Cubs SS Dansby Swanson Drops Honest Quote Amid Wild Card Series vs. Padres
Via the Chicago Tribune’s Meghan Montemurro on X: Dansby Swanson pregame : “At this time of year, it can be challenging because you go so in depth with the other team & trying to navigate what they’re going to do … I think the greatest reminder is if we do what we do best then we feel like we’re a really good baseball team.”
This season, Swanson posted 3.1 bWAR and a .694 OPS with 19 home runs and 69 RBI over 126 games.
Lineups for Cubs-Padres Game 2
Here is the Cubs’ lineup for today:
- Pete Crow-Armstrong CF
- Alex Bregman DH
- Michael Busch 1B
- Seiya Suzuki RF
- Ian Happ LF
- Nico Hoerner 2B
- Matt Shaw 3B
- Carson Kelly C
- Dansby Swanson SS

- Fernando Taits Jr. RF
- Dustin Harris LF
- Manny Machado 3B
- Ty France 1B
- Jackson Merrill CF

- Ethan Salas C
- Austin Hays DH

Chicago Cubs Starting Pitcher
Kevin Gausman will start for the Cubs today.
The Cubs acquired Gausman, 35, from the Toronto Blue Jays for center fielder Brett Bateman and shortstop Ty Southisene on Aug. 2.
Gausman recorded a 4.83 ERA with 57 strikeouts in 50 1/3 innings across nine starts this Chicago this season. He had a 4.38 ERA with 127 strikeouts in 127 1/3 innings over 23 starts with Toronto this year.

item.dc:creator: Tony Crumpton

item.content:encoded:
Dansby Swanson addressed the media at Petco Park ahead of Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series to discuss the Chicago Cubs' mindset following a Game 1 loss.
Watch the video below:
Q. You guys have talked all season long about this team's ability to kind of reset and start anew each new day. Are you seeing that so far today, and how do you think that's going to be able to benefit you guys today?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think we've all -- this whole year we've had opportunities to respond to adversity, and this is obviously no different. We have such a professional group, a group that prides itself on getting better each and every day no matter the circumstance. So business as usual in that regard.
Q. What is it like knowing you guys have Gausman starting tonight, given his experience in big playoff moments like this and just seeing his track record?
DANSBY SWANSON: He's pitched in a lot of big games in his career, in his life. We were thrilled to be able to acquire him at the deadline just knowing that experience and what he brings, the toughness, the pitch ability, and being able to have him on our team to help navigate through moments like this is a big part of why he's here.
He's been so good for us all year in big moments, and I expect nothing different tonight.
Q. From your experience, what's the key in games like today?
DANSBY SWANSON: Really and truly, it's just about being locked in on every pitch, just laying it all out there and understanding that we're at our best when we do what we do best.
At this time of year, it can be challenging because you go so in depth with the other team and trying to navigate what they're going to do, what we're going to do. I think the greatest reminder is, if we do what we do best, then we feel like we're a really good baseball team.
Q. Yesterday Craig went with Pedro at third. Today he goes with Matt Shaw. You saw what Pedro did when you were out. Just what's it like knowing those are the two guys you have behind the main group when something happens with Bregman or happened with you or somebody else?
DANSBY SWANSON: The depth of this group has definitely been a strength, a guy who's able to play multiple positions, able to put together great at-bats off different types of pitchers, and really just the personality piece. Great guys in the clubhouse and the ability to just add to our roster in terms of whether it's hitting left-handed pitching, right-handed pitching, being able to play second base, third base, slide around wherever is needed.
Without them, I doubt that we're in a position that we're in right now. So thankful for those guys, thankful for what they bring every day. Very glad that they're on our team.
Q. We've asked Bregman questions like every day since that day in Cincinnati, and he came back so quickly. Can you just put it into context, like what he's done and kind of what he's playing through and how kind of crazy it is when you take a step back and see what's happened over the past ten days or so?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think, if anyone knows Breggy, some facial fractures weren't going to stop him. He's dedicated to this game. He's dedicated to his craft. He's dedicated to his teammates, trying to find ways each and every day to not only personally get better, but to be able to help guys on the team get better.
It's been so fun being able to be on a team with him, just seeing what he does every day and what he brings to a group. I expect nothing else out of him at this point, doing whatever he can to be able to go out there, take the field. He knows that we're better when he's out there.
Q. Obviously you didn't really get much game action coming back from your injury. Just how have you been feeling with where your swing is at and just your comfort level in the box?
DANSBY SWANSON: Obviously baseball is a game that's meant to be played every day. When you miss a significant amount of time, it presents its own challenges coming back into it. I think kind of somewhat accepting that and going through the rehab process and understanding the position I was going to need to be in in order to get back to be as good as I can be was something that did drive me during that timeout.
It's like unfortunately, but also fortunately, having that time to be able to just kind of reflect and be able to do whatever I can to get back on the field and help this team win baseball games.
That's what I feel is a strength of mine as part of this group, and so thankful to be part of a group that is willing to step up in each and every way and not to overly say that I have to be the one to get things done or whatever. We're a group, we're a team, and we continue to push forward in that way.
Q. What's it been like to see Pete do what he's done this year with the idea that he's still so early in his career and he's got so much more to learn from and use to get better over the years?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think one of the really impressive things about Pete is the thing we've always seen, the physical ability, just the tools that he has, the strength, the defense, the base running. But to be able to really slow the game down this year and understand what he's trying to do at the plate to be able to -- I don't know if we've seen as significant of like a change in like walk rate or swing rate and all those kinds of things as we have with him.
He's just gotten so good at knowing what he's trying to do, how he's trying to execute, and been really stubborn at sticking to that. I think that's one of the big reasons why you've seen his game go into a new level is the ability to like mentally process things much quicker than it was earlier in his career. I think obviously that will only continue to get better.
To be able to do that at such a young age with more or less the different pressures you may have on you and attention on you, he's handled it so gracefully. It's been really, really cool to watch. Obviously having been somewhat in his shoes before and then being on like the older side, the veteran side of things, it's really cool to see him go through that and handle things the way he does.
Q. Obviously you guys have one of the best defenses in baseball, MVP candidate having a crazy, great season, and one of the best offenses. How important is it to take advantage of a season like this when you have the opportunity in the playoffs?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think each year is its own year, right? I think we don't really pay too much attention to those kinds of things. I think this group knows what it's capable of, so it's always reaching for the highest of heights that it can. That's one thing that I do love about this group is the relentless pursuit of really greatness together.
That's something that we've done all year. It's been kind of like a consistent mentality of ours all year. That's why it's so fun to be in positions like this because this is -- you know, being in situations like this is something that can only add to that confidence and to that mentality.
Q. Maybe a dumb question, but you guys from a distance obviously have a phenomenal defense. You've got great defensive players. That's got to be a huge part of it. Do you feel like this team maybe the last couple years compared to other teams you've been on puts an extra emphasis on that at all or goes out of the way to take advantage of the fact that you have the kind of defensive talent you do?
DANSBY SWANSON: It's almost like the last of a dying breed, right? Just like defense, no matter how great we've been offensively and the things we've done on the base pass, defense really is kind of our calling card.
It's interesting because it's not like something I would say that we like go above and beyond to work on it more. Jed and company have put together a great defensive roster obviously because we understand that defense really can change games. When you have Gold Glove-caliber defenders all over the yard, it makes it really tough on teams.
We understand that going out there and doing our part makes it hard for people to score on us. It's really fun to be a part of something like that. Give a lot of credit to the front office for being able to put together a team that is capable of doing more things than just playing defense, but it's wild when you go from really great defenses to not great defenses and like how much it can change things. We've been so consistent at remaining true to ourselves all year.
Q. Yesterday Gausman was saying that you treat this game like any other game except there's all those yellow towels flying around, and it can feel like momentum in these games in the postseason can feel even more real. What's it like managing that side of the game and the postseason?
DANSBY SWANSON: The biggest thing is accepting that it is the same game, right? It's the same rules other than the extra innings if there's not somebody on second base. But it's the same rules.
And being able to embrace that we are prepared and we've just got to go leave it all out there each and every day, each and every pitch, every inning and understanding that things can turn it one swing of the bat, one play in the field, one pitch, and just consistently attacking each and every pitch, whether it's on offense or defense.
Q. The pitching staff has obviously been through a lot this season. Can you just describe what it's been like watching how Counsell, the staff have pieced it together, especially at this point in the season and in a game like this where obviously it's all hands on deck?
DANSBY SWANSON: It's kind of wild when you like kind of ride it out, just the injuries that we've sustained, the things that we've gone through in the pitching department itself. Give a lot of credit to the guys that are here now, obviously Tommy and the rest of the pitching staff for being able to consistently find ways to improve the group and get guys better.
Then you look at just some of the acquisitions and all those kinds of things and really being able to identify traits that are going to play well at this time of year. It's really impressive what Counsell is able to do really putting each guy in a great position to succeed. It sounds simple, but he does it at a really, really high rate. I think it's something that he's really, really good at.
He's done well for the pitching staff, and they've obviously rewarded him in the same way by throwing the ball well. Very thankful for that and the hard work that everyone's done to be able to get to this point. Hopefully we'll go out there and put together a complete performance tonight.

item.content:encoded:
Bryce Harper Reacts to Game-Tying HR After Misplay in Phillies Win vs. Braves in MLB Playoffs G2
Philadelphia Phillies star Bryce Harper had quite the sequence between the bottom of the seventh inning and the top of the eighth during his team's 4-3 win Wednesday
A costly fielding error ultimately led to a pair of Braves' runs, allowing them to take a 3-1 lead. But Harper then followed up Kyle Schwarber's solo homer with one of his own the very next inning, tying the game right back up.
Harper spoke about both moments following the win:
"You've got to flush [the mistake] as quickly as possible knowing that [Braves' pitcher Dylan Lee] is coming into the game," Harper said. "And obviously I was hearing it pretty good from Braves' and Phillies' fans behind the dugout. So gotta show up in that situation. Kyle had a great at-bat and then... I wasn't not trying to hit a homer, I'll tell you that."
Harper primarily played first base this season and shifted to right field after second baseman Luis Arráez—who is unavailable for this series due to a sprained ankle suffered last Thursday—was acquired at the trade deadline, requiring a reshuffling of the infield. He's generally been steady since moving back to the outfield, though Wednesday's error was nearly costly.
And his redemption arc wasn't complete without a few of his teammates chipping in.
There was pitcher Andrew Painter, who came out of the bullpen and threw three scoreless innings, earning the win. Not too shabby for Philadelphia's fifth starter, who isn't accustomed to pitching out of the bullpen.
Or as Harper described Painter's performance: "Absolute dawg mentality, closes the door for us."
And then there was Alec Bohm, who put the Phillies up by a run in the top of the 10th inning with an opposite-field homer.
"No, I didn't," Bohm admitted in his post-game interview on NBC when asked if he knew he hit a homer off the bat. "I don't really know what happened. I was trying to pull the ball off the foul pole and I hit it to right field so, I'll take it."

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] White Sox chase Astros ace Hunter Brown in first inning of Game 2
item.dc:creator: Sportsnet Staff
item.description: After dropping Game 1 of their wild-card series to the Chicago White Sox while throwing a bullpen day, the Houston Astros had to feel a sense of relief knowing they were turning to their ace, Hunter Brown, for Game 2. But as the second inning came around on Wednesday, Brown had already been chased from the contest. item.content:encoded:
After dropping Game 1 of their wild-card series to the Chicago White Sox while throwing a bullpen day, the Houston Astros had to feel a sense of relief knowing they were turning to their ace, Hunter Brown, for Game 2.
But as the second inning came around on Wednesday, Brown had already been chased from the contest.
Chicago sent 10 batters to the plate in a four-run first, tagging Brown for five hits as it looked to win its first playoff series since 2005.
Brown managed to get two outs — both by way of the strikeout — before manager Joe Espada made the move to the bullpen.
White Sox leadoff hitter Sam Antonacci wasted little time putting Brown on his back foot, opening the game with a double that went off Astros left fielder Yordan Alvarez's glove. Kyle Teel then brought home Antonacci with a single, Miguel Vargas reached on an error, Andrew Benintendi scored both with a single and Tristan Peters completed the rally with an RBI single of his own.
Brown left with the bases loaded and two out, but Tuesday's opener, AJ Blubaugh, entered and escaped the jam.
Houston's pitching staff has been ravaged by injuries this season, leaving the 28-year-old Brown and Hayden Wesneski as their lone healthy starters for the playoffs.
With the Astros not clinching their AL West title until the final day of the regular season, they weren't able to line up their pitching staff, which led to the bullpen day in Game 1 before Brown and Wesneski could return on normal rest.
"Having those guys healthy with regular rest, it's super valuable for us," Espdada said before the series began, making Brown's short start all the more costly for an Astros team already needing length from their pitchers.
Brown finished the 2026 regular season with a 3.19 ERA and 124 strikeouts over 107.1 innings. He was also hit by the injury bug earlier in the season, which limited the six-foot-two right-hander to just 20 starts.

item.content:encoded:
Thin MLB crowds in Atlanta, Houston show challenge of selling afternoon Wild Card Series tickets
A late home run secured a playoff win for Atlanta; stadium attendance remains low for scheduled weekday afternoon games
- 1 minuto de lectura'
Austin Riley delivered the first clutch moment of Major League Baseball's playoffs on Tuesday, hitting a go-ahead three-run homer in the eighth inning that pushed the Atlanta Braves over the Philadelphia Phillies for a 5-3 win .
It was an electric scene for fans at Truist Park — at least for those who decided to show up.
There has been a noticeable number of empty seats in Atlanta and Houston for day games during this week's Wild Card Series, with the Braves drawing 30,127 fans for Game 1 on Tuesday that started at 2 p.m. local time, well below the 41,108 capacity. The Astros announced that 34,011 fans attended Tuesday's 4 p.m. Game 1 at Daikin Park, also well below its 41,168-seat limit.
It's not the first time this has happened.
Since MLB permanently expanded the playoffs to a 12-team bracket in 2022, just six of 26 afternoon Wild Card Series games through Tuesday have reached or exceeded stadium capacity. Seven games failed to reach even 85% capacity. The Braves-Phillies game on Tuesday was 73.2% full, which is the lowest since the postseason expanded, according to research from Sportradar.
Game 2 of the Braves-Phillies series had an announced crowd of 37,150 on Wednesday.
The main issue for day games is obvious: It's hard for fans to attend day games during the week — particularly in late September and October — because people have to work and children are back in school. It doesn't help that those game times are announced with only a few days' notice.
Still, it's a less-than-ideal atmosphere for some of the most important contests of the year.
Phillies third baseman Alec Bohm shrugged off the smaller crowds before Wednesday's game, saying his team just wants to win games and advance.
“I don’t think anybody on our team is really focused on how many people are showing up here," Bohm said. "It’s just kind of -- I think, like you said, it’s a 2 o’clock game in the middle of the week, so I think that might have something to do with it.
“That doesn’t take away from what’s going on on the field and kind of the stakes of all that in our minds.”
All three ALWCS games in Cleveland last year between the Guardians and Detroit Tigers started at 1:08 p.m., and none drew more than 30,000 fans. The Tampa Bay Rays had just 19,704 for an ALWCS opener against Texas in 2023 that started at 3:08 p.m., the lowest attendance for a non-COVID MLB postseason game since the 1919 World Series.
MLB declined to comment on the attendance numbers, but the league spreads its wild-card games throughout the day on purpose so they have their own television window and capture the largest viewing audience possible. NBC is paying the league roughly $200 million per year to host “Sunday Night Baseball” and the Wild Card Series during a three-year deal agreed to last November.
The Astros fans who did attend Tuesday's game were in a bit of a foul mood, peppering the team with boos as they fell behind 5-0 by the fifth inning on the way to a 6-3 loss. Astros manager Joe Espada said he understood the fans' frustration but hoped for a better atmosphere on Wednesday.
“I do want our fans to know that we love them and we need them,” Espada said. “They’re part of what we are trying to accomplish here. They’re part of our family.”
AP Sports Writers Charles Odum in Atlanta and Kristie Rieken in Houston contributed to this story.
See AP’s full MLB coverage here

item.content:encoded:
By GLENN GUILBEAU, Tiger Rag Editor
The Pittsburgh Pirates were eliminated from the Major League Baseball Playoffs entering the last week of the regular season last week. That is 11 straight seasons for the franchise and third straight with franchise pitcher Paul Skenes – the No. 1 pick of the MLB Draft in 2023 from LSU.
The Pirates were better in 2026 than in Skenes’ first two seasons as Pittsburgh actually finished above .500 at 82-80 and in third place in the National League Central behind Milwaukee, which had the best regular season record in baseball at 103-59 and the Chicago Cubs at 89-73. Pittsburgh’s record would have been good enough to win the American League West, which Houston took at 81-81 to become the first team in MLB history to win a division with a non-winning record in a non-shortened season. The Texas Rangers were second at 80-82.
In 2025, the Pirates finished 71-91, and they were 76-86 in 2024.
When Skenes won National League Rookie of the Year in 2024 at 11-3 with a 1.96 ERA and started the first of two straight All-Star games, Pittsburgh averaged 1.35 runs a game with Skenes on the mound. In 2025 when Skenes took the National League Cy Young with a 10-10 mark and 1.96 ERA, he got 3.4 runs a game.
This season, Pittsburgh’s offense improved to 4.73 runs a game and 4.74 for Skenes, but he didn’t keep up his end. His ERA ballooned, for him, to 3.82 as he finished 10-11 on the season.
“Their ace’s struggles offered a reminder of one reason why a ticket won’t be punched,” Colin Beazley of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette wrote as the season neared the end.
The main reason for Skenes’ skid has been, according to most accounts, his drop in velocity from 98.8 as a rookie to 98.2 in 2025 and to 96.8 this season.
“It’s been frustrating,” Skenes told FOX Sports late in the season. “But the thing I’ve kind of realized is that I do everything I can. There’s an answer there somewhere. The velo is down. We see all the numbers. We can try to address it. We can do all that. To some extent, it’s kind of just how it is.”
Once the season ended last week, though, Skenes, 24, got a little more detailed in an exclusive interview with the Pittsburgh-Post Gazette and pointed to a variable. He pitched shortly before the season for Team USA in the World Baseball Classic last March, going 2-0 with a 1.08 ERA in eight and a third innings. That’s not a lot, and Skenes admitted to having some mechanical issues throughout the season. But he said he believes the pre-season WBC pitching may have triggered his issues in 2026 after no such pitching before his first two seasons.
“There are a lot of other factors, so I don’t want to put everything on the WBC,” Skenes told the Post-Gazette in an extensive interview published this past Monday. “But I feel like that was kind of the root of it a little bit. Usually, that time of year (in March at spring training), you’re kind of ramping up, and it’s a little bit slow. You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body. You’re topping at 97, and then the next you’re 98, 99. And that’s wasn’t the case this year. Looking back, I don’t think that (pitching in the WBC) really helped.”
Skenes’ average fastball velocity in the 2026 season was 96.8 mph, down from 98.1 in 2025 and 98.8 in 2024. His fastball dropped to a career “slow” 95.7 mph this past August in a game against Miami and averaged 96.1 in his last start on Sept. 25 against Kansas City.
His velocity was up and down through much of the season as was his consistency. He would have a poor outing, then a good one. He had three consecutive quality starts in mid-June. But from June 26 through August 5, he had a 6.26 ERA in eight starts with an uncharacteristic 3.9 walks per nine innings when his career average for walks was 2.2 per nine.
But even when he was pitching well, such as a 1.09 ERA over eight starts last April and May, he said something wasn’t right.
“Even then, I didn’t feel like I had my delivery,” Skenes told the Post-Gazette. “It’s just weird. It’s easier to kind of put your finger on it after the fact than it is in the moment.”
Skenes hopes to enter 2027 with no baggage.
“It definitely affected the year,” he said of pitching in the WBC. “It definitely didn’t make things easier.”
And sometimes little things make a difference.
“Everything is just having awareness of your hand at release,” Skenes told FOX shortly before the season ended. “It’s amazing how small things can be up the chain to throw that off. But looking at my assessments, nothing crazy has happened. What has happened this year, probably for that stretch in June through the beginning of August, was the velocity went down.”
That will obviously be what Skenes and the Pirates focus on before the 2027 season, which will be his first under the arbitration window. His contract runs out in the 2029 season.
“We’ll try to address it,” he said. “But you also have to understand what’s in your control and what’s not in your control. That was kind of not in my control. The velo goes up and down sometimes. Nothing has really explained my velocity drop. So, I’m not going to lose any sleep over it.”
That may be because of a conversation Skenes had with Detroit Tiger Justin Verlander late in the season. Verlander, a 10-time All-Star, five-time strikeout leader and three-time Cy Young winner who was the 2006 rookie of the year, announced during the 2026 season that ’26 would be his last at age 43.
Verlander told Skenes that his velocity mysteriously dropped in his third full season at Detroit in 2008 as Skenes did in his third year in 2026.
“He was like, ‘My third year, I just lost my velo. I was completely healthy. It kind of just went away, and then it came back,’” Skenes said.
The Baseball Savant velocity tracker confirmed Verlander dropped to 94.3 in his third season in 2008, then rose to 96.3 in 2009 and remained up through most of his career.
“I was like, ‘You know what? That’s kind of good to hear,’” Skenes said he told Verlander. “It’s not just me.”
And it likely was, partly, the WBC action.

item.content:encoded:
La trayectoria de Jonathan Aranda representa un recorrido destacado desde el beisbol infantil de Tijuana hasta los escenarios más importantes de las Grandes Ligas. El tijuanense pasó de formarse en los campos de la Liga Municipal de Tijuana a convertirse en pieza fundamental de los Tampa Bay Rays, equipo que aseguró su lugar en las Series Divisionales de los Playoffs de la MLB.
Durante la temporada regular 2026, Aranda tuvo un papel protagonista dentro de la ofensiva de Tampa Bay. El primera base e infielder mostró consistencia con el bate y terminó la campaña con un promedio de .277, además de sumar 156 imparables, 22 cuadrangulares y 92 carreras producidas, cifras que reflejan su importancia en el orden ofensivo de los Rays.
Su rendimiento fue determinante para que Tampa Bay alcanzara los playoffs con la mira puesta en avanzar a las siguientes rondas. Para Aranda, la clasificación representa otro paso importante en una carrera que comenzó en el beisbol tijuanense y que ahora lo coloca frente a uno de los mayores retos de su trayectoria. Aquí en Heraldo Deportes te contamos sus inicios y cómo llegó a Grandes Ligas.
Así fueron los humildes inicios de Jonathan Aranda en el beisbol de Tijuana
Jonathan Aranda encontró en el béisbol una oportunidad para mantenerse alejado de los entornos de violencia en Tijuana y construir un camino ligado al deporte. Nacido el 23 de mayo de 1998 en Baja California, comenzó a jugar desde pequeño con el respaldo de sus padres, Humberto Aranda y Ventura, quienes veían en esta actividad una forma de fomentar la disciplina y mantenerlo protegido. Con el paso de los años, aquella iniciativa familiar se convirtió en el inicio de una carrera que lo llevaría hasta las Grandes Ligas.
Durante su infancia, Aranda desarrolló su talento en las ligas infantiles y juveniles de Tijuana, donde destacó especialmente en la Liga Municipal. En esos campos también forjó una amistad con Alejandro Kirk, otro pelotero tijuanense que alcanzaría el máximo nivel del béisbol profesional. Ambos compartieron sus primeros pasos en el diamante y, con el tiempo, transformaron aquellos años de formación en una trayectoria que los llevaría a representar a México en la MLB.
Te puede interesar: Playoffs MLB 2026: Así puedes VER EN VIVO los juegos entre Yankees y Red Sox de Grandes Ligas
La historia de cómo Jonathan Aranda llegó a Grandes Ligas
El camino profesional de Jonathan Aranda comenzó con los Toros de Tijuana, donde fue identificado como uno de los jóvenes talentos de la región. El tijuanense pasó cerca de dos años dentro del sistema de desarrollo del club, trabajando principalmente en su capacidad de contacto y preparación ofensiva. En 2016 tuvo actividad con los Toros de Moroleón en la Liga Invernal Mexicana, una etapa que le permitió adquirir experiencia y llamar la atención de organizaciones de Grandes Ligas.
Su oportunidad con los Tampa Bay Rays surgió durante una sesión de visoría realizada en Tijuana en 2015. Los cazatalentos habían acudido para observar a Randy Arozarena, quien entrenaba con los Toros, y terminaron siguiendo de cerca el desempeño de Aranda. El bateador tijuanense convenció por su técnica y capacidad ofensiva, por lo que los Rays decidieron firmarlo por un bono de 130 mil dólares, dando inicio a su recorrido por las ligas menores. Siete años después, en 2022, Aranda debutó en la MLB y comenzó una nueva etapa de su carrera en el máximo nivel del béisbol.

It will be either the Atlanta Braves or the Philadelphia Phillies. Amid the MLB playoffs, the Dodgers made a few roster moves in preparation for their upcoming series. item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are in full swing, as Wild Card matchups began this week.
For the Los Angeles Dodgers, they are still awaiting their opponent for the NLDS. It will be either the Atlanta Braves or the Philadelphia Phillies.
Amid the MLB playoffs, the Dodgers made a few roster moves in preparation for their upcoming series.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Announce Tyler Mahle News After Dramatic Phillies Game
Los Angeles Dodgers Make 3 Roster Changes
The Dodgers do know that they will begin their quest for a three-peat on Saturday, October 3.
In the meantime, here are the three roster moves the team made, per the team’s transactions tracker:
“Los Angeles Dodgers activated RHP Edgardo Henriquez from the 15-day injured list.”
“Los Angeles Dodgers recalled LHP Ronan Kopp from Oklahoma City Comets.”
“Los Angeles Dodgers recalled SS Hyeseong Kim from Oklahoma City Comets.”
The most notable roster move of the trio is Edgardo Henriquez being activated from the 15-day IL, which could be a huge boost to the Dodgers’ bullpen. However, he still needs to be announced on the Dodgers’ NLDS roster, which has not been made public yet.
As for Hyeseong Kim, he could be a pinch-runner option if the Dodgers opt to go that route.
More MLB on Heavy: Chicago Cubs Announce Interesting Seiya Suzuki Decision Before MLB Playoffs
What Do Roster Moves Mean for Los Angeles Dodgers Playoff Chances?
If Henriquez can go for the Los Angeles Dodgers’ relief corps, that is a huge boost because he has been one of the team’s breakout pitchers and a highly dependable reliever.
As for the other two moves, they might not be noticeable now, but could play a role down the line.
Ronan Kopp being recalled to the 40-man roster is likely in case of an emergency, but if the Dodgers advance past the NLDS, there’s a slight chance he could be added to the official postseason roster.
Hyeseong Kim is a player who could pay slight dividends on the bases if manager Dave Roberts opts to use him in the late innings as a pinch-runner option.
